subtopics.title: Systems across scales, from a cell to a planet

subtopics.title: Drawing a system's boundary

subtopics.title: Open vs closed systems

subtopics.title: Inputs and outputs

subtopics.title: Tracing matter and energy through a system

subtopics.title: Choosing a boundary for a purpose

subtopics.title: Why scientists build models

subtopics.title: Diagrams and flowcharts as models

subtopics.title: Physical and digital models
subtopics.idea: Physical and digital models fail in different directions.

subtopics.title: What a model leaves out on purpose

subtopics.title: Interactions among Earth's four spheres

subtopics.title: Modeling an Earth-system event

subtopics.title: SI units and measurement

subtopics.title: Organizing and graphing data

subtopics.title: Claim, evidence and reasoning

B1.title: Cells: the basic unit of life

subtopics.title: Cell theory
subtopics.idea: Cell theory says every living thing is made of cells, cells come only from other cells, and the cell is the smallest living unit.
subtopics.design: Historical microscope bench: swap 1665 Hooke, 1674 Leeuwenhoek and modern optics over the same six specimens; resolving power (Abbe limit d=lambda/2NA) is real, so each scope reveals only what it physically can. Student builds cell theory from what is actually visible. Fraud to avoid: showing modern images through a 1665 lens.

subtopics.title: Discovering cells
subtopics.idea: Cells were discovered because instruments got better, not because anyone reasoned them out.
subtopics.design: Same bench, driven by numerical aperture: student raises NA and wavelength and watches cork-cell walls resolve at ~1.4 um then bacteria at ~0.4 um. Measures smallest resolvable feature vs NA against the real curve. Fraud: a magnification slider that just scales a bitmap.

subtopics.title: Living vs nonliving
subtopics.idea: Living things do seven measurable things; a candle or crystal does some but never all.
subtopics.design: Test bench: run respiration (CO2 with bromothymol), growth over days, response to stimulus, waste output on candle flame, salt crystal, seed, yeast. Each test is a real measurement over time; the verdict is computed from the tally, never labelled in advance.

subtopics.title: Unicellular organisms
subtopics.idea: One cell can do everything an organism needs: eat, move, expel water, divide.
subtopics.design: Live Paramecium/Euglena under the objective: contractile vacuole fills and fires on a real osmotic clock (rate rises in fresh water), cilia drive real motion, food vacuoles form. Student times the vacuole against salinity. Fraud: a looping animation indifferent to the salt dial.

subtopics.title: Multicellular organisms
subtopics.idea: Many cells let a body specialise — but only if they stay supplied.
subtopics.design: Diffusion-limited tissue: a slab of cells consuming oxygen with Fick's law supply from the surface; student adds thickness and watches the core go hypoxic at the real ~1 mm limit, then adds a vessel and sees it rescued. Measures depth of the living layer.

subtopics.title: Microscopic scale
subtopics.idea: Cells are measured in micrometres, and scale is a ladder you can climb by tens.
subtopics.design: Zoom ladder with a true metric bar: 1 m human, 1 mm sand, 100 um egg, 10 um cell, 1 um bacterium, 100 nm virus, all at honest relative size with a break glyph when a step leaves the screen. Student places unknown specimens on the ladder by measuring them.

subtopics.title: Cell membrane
subtopics.idea: The membrane decides what crosses, and it lets water move to even out concentration.
subtopics.design: Osmosis bench: real semi-permeable membrane between two chambers, solute impermeant, water flux J = Lp*(sigma*RT*dC); student sets concentrations and watches level and cell volume change, plots flux vs gradient. A visible potato core shrinks or swells to match. Fraud: swelling that is not tied to the numbers.

subtopics.title: Cell wall
subtopics.idea: A wall lets a plant cell take in water without bursting — turgor is a pressure you can read.
subtopics.design: Same osmosis rig with the wall toggled on: with the wall, turgor pressure climbs and flux stops at equilibrium; without it the animal cell lyses. Student reads turgor in kPa and finds the wilting point. The wall toggle is structural.

subtopics.title: Nucleus
subtopics.idea: The nucleus holds the instructions; remove it and the cell runs down.
subtopics.design: Enucleation experiment on Acetabularia (the classic): student cuts and grafts, and the cap that regrows follows the nucleus's species, not the stalk's, on a real protein-decay clock. Measures days to cap and which form appears.

subtopics.title: Mitochondria
subtopics.idea: Mitochondria release energy from food using oxygen, and hard-working cells hold more of them.
subtopics.design: Respirometer: cell type (muscle, liver, skin) sets mitochondrial density; student sets workload and reads real O2 consumption and CO2 output, ATP per second, and watches the deficit when demand outruns supply. Fraud: an ATP number not tied to O2 drawn.

subtopics.title: Chloroplasts
subtopics.idea: Chloroplasts build sugar from light and CO2 — and respiration never stops underneath.
subtopics.design: Two-flow leaf chamber: photosynthesis follows a light-response curve, respiration runs day and night; student finds the compensation point where net O2 is zero. Measures net and gross rates separately — the whole lesson is that they are different.

subtopics.title: Relating structure to whole-cell function
subtopics.idea: An organelle's shape is its job: fold a membrane and you buy surface area.
subtopics.design: Build-a-cell bench where each organelle's geometry feeds a real budget: cristae folding sets ATP ceiling, thylakoid stacking sets light capture, surface-to-volume sets exchange. Student assembles a cell for a stated job and tests it against a load. Fraud: decorative organelles.

subtopics.title: The organizational hierarchy
subtopics.idea: Life is organised in levels, and each level does something the level below cannot.
subtopics.design: Level ladder driven by one working body: student zooms cell to tissue to organ to system to organism, and at each level a real capability appears (one muscle cell twitches; a tissue lifts; an organ pumps). Measures force and flow at each level.

subtopics.title: Cell specialization
subtopics.idea: Cells specialise, trading general ability for one job done well.
subtopics.design: Differentiation bench: a stem cell given signals becomes nerve, muscle, or red cell; each then scores on conduction speed, force, and oxygen carried. Student sees each specialist win one column and lose the others. Fraud: a specialist that is best at everything.

subtopics.title: Tissues
subtopics.idea: A tissue is many like cells acting together, and together they pull harder than the sum suggests.
subtopics.design: Tissue pull rig: student adds aligned muscle fibres and measures force; alignment angle matters (cos theta), so a disordered sheet underperforms. Reads force in newtons against fibre count and alignment.

subtopics.title: Organs
subtopics.idea: An organ is different tissues built into one machine with one job.
subtopics.design: Heart build: student assembles muscle, valve and conductive tissue; each missing piece produces a specific, named failure (no valves = backflow, no conduction = fibrillation) measured as cardiac output in L/min.

subtopics.title: Organ systems
subtopics.idea: An organ system links organs into a supply chain, and a break anywhere starves the end.
subtopics.design: Whole-system loop with real flows: student severs one link and traces the shortfall downstream with measurements, never a message. Same chain-of-cause discipline as the aquarium exemplar.

subtopics.title: The organism as the whole system
subtopics.idea: The organism is the level where all systems must balance at once.
subtopics.design: Whole-body dashboard: exercise load drives coupled circulatory, respiratory and thermal models; student must keep every variable in range at once and discovers the trade-offs. Failure states are real (hyperthermia, hypoxia).

subtopics.title: Digestive system
subtopics.idea: Digestion breaks food into pieces small enough to cross into blood.
subtopics.design: Gut tube with real enzyme kinetics: amylase, pepsin at pH 2, lipase with bile; student sets pH and time and measures how much of each macronutrient is actually absorbed. Wrong pH genuinely stalls the enzyme. Fraud: absorption that ignores chemistry.

subtopics.title: Excretory system
subtopics.idea: The kidney keeps what the body needs and dumps the rest, by filtering then reclaiming.
subtopics.design: Nephron bench: filtration by pressure, then reabsorption with real transport maxima (glucose Tm ~ 375 mg/min); student raises blood glucose and finds the spill point where sugar appears in urine. Measures filtrate and urine composition.

subtopics.title: Circulatory system
subtopics.idea: Blood is a delivery loop, and pressure is what keeps it moving.
subtopics.design: Circulatory loop with resistance and compliance: student changes vessel radius and reads flow via Poiseuille (r^4 dependence is the lesson), sees pressure drop across beds and the failure when a vessel narrows.

subtopics.title: Respiratory system
subtopics.idea: Breathing swaps gases across a huge folded surface driven by pressure differences.
subtopics.design: Lung bench: diaphragm sets thoracic pressure, air flows down the gradient, alveolar surface area sets diffusion; student compares healthy vs emphysema (fewer, larger alveoli) and measures O2 saturation reached per breath.

subtopics.title: Muscular system
subtopics.idea: Muscles pull, never push, so they work in opposing pairs.
subtopics.design: Arm rig with real torque: student contracts biceps or triceps and measures joint angle, load lifted and torque; trying to push with a muscle simply does nothing. Fatigue accumulates on a real ATP budget.

subtopics.title: Nervous system
subtopics.idea: Nerves carry fast electrical signals, and speed depends on the fibre.
subtopics.design: Conduction bench: student picks fibre diameter and myelination and measures real conduction velocity (myelinated ~50-120 m/s vs unmyelinated ~1 m/s) over a measured distance with a timer. Fraud: a fixed 'fast' animation.

subtopics.title: Digestion and circulation together
subtopics.idea: Digestion is pointless without circulation to carry the nutrients away.
subtopics.design: Coupled gut-blood model: absorbed glucose enters a bloodstream that distributes it; student cuts the blood supply to the villi and watches absorption itself stall (the gradient collapses). Measures glucose delivered to muscle.

subtopics.title: Circulation and respiration together
subtopics.idea: Circulation and breathing form one oxygen chain from air to cell.
subtopics.design: Coupled loop: alveolar O2 -> haemoglobin saturation curve -> delivery to working muscle; student raises workload and finds which link limits first. Measures O2 delivered vs consumed.

subtopics.title: Nervous and muscular systems together
subtopics.idea: A movement is a signal that becomes a force.
subtopics.design: Catch-a-ball rig: real signal travel time down the arm plus muscle activation delay sets whether the hand closes in time; student changes distance and speed and measures the miss. Reaction time is computed, never fixed.

subtopics.title: The excretory system and internal balance
subtopics.idea: The body holds its internal conditions steady by constantly correcting them.
subtopics.design: Water-balance loop: intake, sweat, urine and ADH feedback with a real setpoint; student stresses it with heat or drinking and watches the correction, its lag, and the overshoot when the loop is slow.

subtopics.title: Case study: the body during exercise
subtopics.idea: Under exercise every system shifts at once, and they must shift together.
subtopics.design: Exercise session: student sets intensity and duration; heart rate, ventilation, temperature, glycogen and lactate all run as coupled stocks. Reads the whole dashboard and finds the sustainable ceiling.

subtopics.title: Interactions among body systems, generalized
subtopics.idea: Systems interact through shared quantities — cut one and the others feel it.
subtopics.design: Generalised body board: eight systems, explicit couplings; student cuts one coupling arrow and traces exactly which downstream measurements move and which do not. Same honesty rule as A1.3.

subtopics.title: Sensory receptors and stimuli
subtopics.idea: A receptor turns one kind of stimulus into a nerve signal, and it has a threshold.
subtopics.design: Receptor bench: student applies pressure, light, heat, sound at measured intensities; firing rate follows a real threshold-and-saturation curve per receptor type. Measures spikes per second vs stimulus.

subtopics.title: The path of a signal to the brain
subtopics.idea: A signal travels a definite path and takes measurable time.
subtopics.design: Path tracer: stimulus at the fingertip, timed relay through nerve, spinal cord, brain; student measures total latency and sees which segment dominates. Distances and velocities are real.

subtopics.title: Processing information in the brain
subtopics.idea: The brain interprets signals — the same input can be read two ways.
subtopics.design: Perception bench: identical sensory input, different context; student sees the interpretation flip while the input trace stays identical. The trace is shown so the student can verify the input never changed.

subtopics.title: Voluntary and reflex responses
subtopics.idea: A reflex skips the brain, which is why it is faster.
subtopics.design: Two-path rig: reflex arc through the cord vs voluntary path through the brain, both timed on real distances; student measures the ~100 ms difference. Fraud: labelling one 'fast' without timing it.

subtopics.title: Memory and stored information
subtopics.idea: Memory is stored information that decays unless it is rehearsed.
subtopics.design: Recall bench: real forgetting curve; student rehearses at chosen intervals and measures retention days later, discovering spacing beats cramming — computed, not asserted.

subtopics.title: Stimulus to response to memory, together
subtopics.idea: Stimulus, response and memory form one loop that changes with experience.
subtopics.design: Full loop: repeated stimulus produces habituation or sensitisation via a real synaptic-strength model; student runs trials and measures the response changing over time.

subtopics.title: Forms of energy
subtopics.idea: Energy comes in forms that can be counted in joules, whatever the form.
subtopics.design: Energy audit bench: student tags kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, electrical in one working machine; every tag reads joules from the model's own state, and the total is displayed. Fraud: labels not tied to state.

subtopics.title: Kinetic energy
subtopics.idea: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed — double the speed, quadruple the energy.
subtopics.design: Trolley and crush block: student launches at measured speeds and measures crush depth; the v-squared law emerges from the plotted runs, not from a formula on screen.

subtopics.title: Potential energy
subtopics.idea: Stored energy depends on height (or stretch) and can be released on demand.
subtopics.design: Lift-and-drop rig plus spring bench: student lifts a mass a measured height, reads mgh, releases, and watches it convert; spring stores half-k-x-squared. Both measured from state.

subtopics.title: Energy transfer and transformation
subtopics.idea: Energy transfers between objects and transforms between forms — usually several at once.
subtopics.design: Chain machine: hand crank to generator to bulb to warm air, each stage a real efficiency; student follows the joules and sees where they go at each step.

subtopics.title: Conservation of energy, introduced
subtopics.idea: Energy is never lost — the total stays put once you count the heat.
subtopics.design: Closed-boundary experiment: student draws the boundary around the machine and the room; inside the full boundary the total is flat to the last joule, outside it appears to vanish. The ledger is computed.

subtopics.title: Tracking energy through everyday examples
subtopics.idea: You can follow energy through any everyday chain if you keep a ledger.
subtopics.design: Everyday chains (toaster, bicycle, torch): student picks a chain and tracks joules through each stage with a real efficiency, ending at low-grade heat.

subtopics.title: Matter is made of particles
subtopics.idea: Everything is made of particles too small to see, and that explains what matter does.
subtopics.design: Brownian-motion microscope: real random-walk model where pollen jitter scales with temperature and particle size; student measures displacement vs time and finds the square-root law.

subtopics.title: Evidence for particle motion
subtopics.idea: Particle motion is not a story — it leaves measurable traces.
subtopics.design: Diffusion race: scent or dye spreads with a real diffusion coefficient that rises with temperature and falls with molecular mass; student times arrival at a measured distance.

subtopics.title: Particle movement in solids, liquids and gases
subtopics.idea: Solids, liquids and gases differ in how their particles are held and how they move.
subtopics.design: Particle box with real intermolecular potential: student sets temperature and watches the state change emerge from the model; measures mean free path, density and whether shape is retained.

subtopics.title: Temperature as average kinetic energy
subtopics.idea: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of the particles.
subtopics.design: Speed-distribution bench: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution live; student raises temperature and watches the whole distribution shift, and reads that average KE tracks absolute temperature exactly.

subtopics.title: Temperature vs total thermal energy
subtopics.idea: A bathtub holds more thermal energy than a spark, even though the spark is hotter.
subtopics.design: Two-object comparison: student sets mass and temperature for a spark and a bath; reads temperature and total thermal energy separately and finds they rank oppositely. This IS the subtopic.

subtopics.title: Measuring temperature
subtopics.idea: A thermometer reads its own temperature, once it has reached equilibrium with what it touches.
subtopics.design: Thermometer bench: real thermal mass and time constant; student plunges a cold thermometer into warm water and watches the reading approach the truth on an exponential, and sees a heavy probe cool a small sample.

subtopics.title: Energy flows hot to cold
subtopics.idea: Energy always flows from hotter to colder, never the reverse on its own.
subtopics.design: Two-block contact: real conduction; student sets both temperatures and finds the flow direction always follows the gradient, and stops at equality — never reverses.

subtopics.title: Conduction
subtopics.idea: Conduction moves energy through a material without moving the material.
subtopics.design: Rod bench: Fourier's law with real conductivities; student times wax markers melting along copper, steel, glass and plots position vs time.

subtopics.title: Convection
subtopics.idea: In fluids, warm parts rise and set up a circulating current.
subtopics.design: Convection tank: buoyancy from real density-temperature relation drives a cell; student heats one corner and traces the loop with dye, measuring speed vs heater power.

subtopics.title: Radiation
subtopics.idea: Radiation crosses empty space and depends on surface and temperature.
subtopics.design: Vacuum-gap rig: Stefan-Boltzmann with emissivity; student compares black, white and shiny surfaces at measured temperatures and reads received power.

subtopics.title: Conductors and insulators
subtopics.idea: Materials differ hugely in how well they pass heat, and that is why we choose them.
subtopics.design: Material comparison rig: same gradient, different samples; student ranks by measured heat flow and discovers metals and air differ by ~10000x.

subtopics.title: Thermal equilibrium
subtopics.idea: Left alone, everything in contact ends at one temperature.
subtopics.design: Multi-body equilibrium: three objects of different mass, material and start temperature; student predicts the final shared temperature and checks it against the real weighted result.

subtopics.title: Effect of material type on temperature change
subtopics.idea: Different materials need different amounts of energy for the same temperature rise.
subtopics.design: Specific-heat bench: identical heater, identical mass, different materials; student measures the temperature-time slope for water, oil, aluminium, sand and derives c.

subtopics.title: Effect of mass on temperature change
subtopics.idea: More mass means slower heating for the same heater.
subtopics.design: Mass series: same material and heater, varying mass; student plots slope vs mass and finds the inverse relation.

subtopics.title: Planning a fair test investigation
subtopics.idea: A fair test changes one thing and holds everything else fixed.
subtopics.design: Fair-test planner over the same heater rig: student locks variables; the model genuinely confounds the result if two vary at once, and the confound is measured, not warned about.

subtopics.title: Collecting and organizing temperature-time data
subtopics.idea: Good data collection means a table you can actually plot.
subtopics.design: Data bench: student chooses interval and duration and records real runs; too-coarse sampling genuinely hides the curve, and the miss is measurable.

subtopics.title: Analyzing and interpreting data
subtopics.idea: Analysis means finding the pattern in the numbers, not eyeballing the picture.
subtopics.design: Analysis bench on the student's own runs: gradient, best fit and residuals computed from their recorded rows.

subtopics.title: Constructing an explanation from evidence
subtopics.idea: An explanation must be built from the evidence you actually collected.
subtopics.design: Explanation builder: student assembles claim, evidence rows and reasoning; the fit is scored against whether the cited rows actually support the claim, computed.

subtopics.title: Choosing materials to control heat transfer
subtopics.idea: Choosing a material is choosing a heat-transfer rate.
subtopics.design: Material chooser feeding a real cup model: each choice sets conductivity, emissivity and thickness; student sees the predicted hold time before building.

subtopics.title: Defining the design problem
subtopics.idea: A design problem is only solvable once criteria and constraints are stated as numbers.
subtopics.design: Brief bench: student sets target hold time, budget and size limits; the model refuses vague targets and scores only against the stated numbers.

subtopics.title: Designing and building a device
subtopics.idea: Building means turning a specification into a thing that exists.
subtopics.design: Cup builder: layers, thickness, lid, gap; the assembled geometry feeds the real thermal model — every choice changes the measured curve.

subtopics.title: Testing a device and collecting data
subtopics.idea: A test produces data, and the data is the verdict.
subtopics.design: Test rig: student runs their cup with a real thermometer and timer, recording the cooling curve against the stated criterion.

subtopics.title: Comparing competing designs
subtopics.idea: Comparing designs means comparing measurements under identical conditions.
subtopics.design: Head-to-head: two student designs run in the same ambient with the same start temperature; the comparison is the measured curves.

subtopics.title: Redesigning based on evidence
subtopics.idea: Redesign is evidence-driven: change what the data says is failing.
subtopics.design: Iteration bench: student sees where their loss happened (conduction vs radiation vs lid gap, itemised in watts) and changes that, then re-tests.

D1.title: Earth's water and the water cycle

subtopics.title: Earth's water reservoirs
subtopics.idea: Almost all of Earth's water is ocean; the fresh liquid part is a sliver.
subtopics.design: Reservoir bench with true volumes (1.34e9 km3 ocean, ice, groundwater, lakes, atmosphere) drawn at honest relative scale with a break glyph; student pours between reservoirs and the totals must balance. Fraud: pie slices resized for legibility.

subtopics.title: Evaporation and condensation
subtopics.idea: Water leaves a surface as vapour and returns as liquid when the air cannot hold it.
subtopics.design: Evaporation/condensation chamber: real saturation vapour pressure (Magnus), student sets temperature, humidity and wind and measures evaporation rate and the exact dew point where condensation starts.

subtopics.title: Precipitation, runoff and infiltration
subtopics.idea: Rain that lands either runs off or soaks in, and the ground decides which.
subtopics.design: Rainfall plot: real infiltration (Horton) vs surface type; student sets intensity and soil and measures runoff vs infiltration split, and finds the intensity where the soil is overwhelmed.

subtopics.title: Transpiration and the biological piece of the cycle
subtopics.idea: Plants move a large share of the water from soil back to air.
subtopics.design: Transpiration bench: real stomatal conductance responding to light, humidity and wind; student compares bare soil, grass and a tree over a day and measures litres returned.

subtopics.title: Two drivers: solar energy and gravity
subtopics.idea: Two forces drive the whole cycle: the Sun lifts water, gravity brings it down.
subtopics.design: Driver toggles: student turns off solar input or gravity and watches which half of the cycle stops; every flow is tagged with its driver. The cycle cannot run on one alone.

subtopics.title: Residence time and the water cycle as a system
subtopics.idea: Water stays in some reservoirs for days and others for millennia.
subtopics.design: Residence-time bench: stock divided by outflow computed live; student tags a droplet and times its stay in atmosphere (~9 days) vs deep ocean (~1000 y). Measured, not stated.

subtopics.title: Composition of the atmosphere
subtopics.idea: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with trace gases that matter far beyond their share.
subtopics.design: Composition bench: student samples air, separates it, and measures each fraction; then removes a trace gas and sees its outsized effect in a coupled radiative model.

subtopics.title: Layers of the atmosphere
subtopics.idea: The atmosphere has layers defined by whether temperature rises or falls with height.
subtopics.design: Ascent profile: real US Standard Atmosphere lapse rates; student flies a probe and plots temperature vs altitude, finding each inversion that defines a layer boundary.

subtopics.title: Air pressure
subtopics.idea: Air has weight, and pressure is the weight of the air above you.
subtopics.design: Barometer bench: hydrostatic integration; student climbs and reads pressure falling, and measures the column mass above each altitude.

subtopics.title: Pressure, temperature and density together
subtopics.idea: Pressure, temperature and density are locked together — fix two and the third follows.
subtopics.design: Gas-law bench for air parcels: student sets any two and the third is computed; tries to set all three and the model refuses. That refusal IS the lesson.

subtopics.title: Why warm air rises
subtopics.idea: Warm air rises because it is less dense than the air around it.
subtopics.design: Buoyancy bench: parcel density from the ideal gas law vs environment; student heats a parcel and measures buoyant acceleration, and finds the neutral level where it stops.

subtopics.title: Temperature
subtopics.idea: Air temperature is measured in shade, because sunlight heats the thermometer, not the air.
subtopics.design: Thermometer siting rig: real radiative heating on the bulb; student compares sun-exposed vs screened readings and measures the error.

subtopics.title: Air pressure and the barometer
subtopics.idea: A barometer's trend predicts weather better than its value.
subtopics.design: Barometer over a passing system: student records pressure over hours and finds falling pressure precedes the front, measured against the arriving weather.

subtopics.title: Humidity and dew point
subtopics.idea: Dew point tells you when the air must give up its water.
subtopics.design: Wet/dry bulb bench: real psychrometry; student measures both and computes relative humidity and dew point, then cools the air to that point and watches condensation begin exactly there.

subtopics.title: Precipitation
subtopics.idea: Rain is measured as a depth, and depth times area gives volume.
subtopics.design: Rain gauge: student collects over a storm, reads depth in mm, and computes the volume over a measured roof — the number is startling and computed.

subtopics.title: Wind: speed and direction
subtopics.idea: Wind has both a speed and a direction, and both must be recorded.
subtopics.design: Anemometer and vane: real cup response; student measures speed and bearing over time and plots a wind rose from their own rows.

subtopics.title: Reading a weather station together
subtopics.idea: A station's instruments together tell a story no single one can.
subtopics.design: Full station: student reads all instruments and must diagnose the incoming weather; the correct diagnosis needs at least three instruments to agree.

subtopics.title: Air masses and source regions
subtopics.idea: An air mass takes on the character of where it formed.
subtopics.design: Source-region bench: student parks an air mass over ocean, desert or ice for a residence time and measures the temperature and humidity it acquires, then moves it.

subtopics.title: High- and low-pressure systems
subtopics.idea: Air spirals into lows and out of highs, and that decides the weather.
subtopics.design: Pressure-system bench: real pressure-gradient plus Coriolis; student sets a high or low and traces the circulation, measuring convergence and the cloud it causes.

subtopics.title: Cold fronts
subtopics.idea: A cold front shoves warm air up steeply, so the weather is violent and brief.
subtopics.design: Front bench: real frontal slope (~1:50) and lifting; student watches the cold wedge arrive and measures the temperature drop, pressure kick and rainfall burst.

subtopics.title: Warm fronts
subtopics.idea: A warm front slides up gently, so the weather is long and mild.
subtopics.design: Same bench, shallow slope (~1:200): student measures the long approach, layered cloud sequence and steady rain, comparing directly against the cold-front run.

subtopics.title: Occluded and stationary fronts
subtopics.idea: When a cold front catches a warm one, the warm air is lifted clear of the ground.
subtopics.design: Occlusion bench: two fronts with different speeds; student runs until the faster catches the slower and measures the warm sector being pinched off the surface.

subtopics.title: Collecting data to track a front
subtopics.idea: You can track a front by taking readings at several places over time.
subtopics.design: Station network: student reads six stations hourly and plots the front's position and speed from their own data — the front is never drawn for them.

subtopics.title: Angle of sunlight and latitude
subtopics.idea: Sunlight arriving at an angle spreads the same energy over more ground.
subtopics.design: Beam-spreading bench: real cosine law; student tilts the surface and measures irradiance in W/m2 and the lit area, finding the trade.

subtopics.title: Land versus water heating rates
subtopics.idea: Water heats and cools far more slowly than land.
subtopics.design: Side-by-side heating: real specific heats and mixing depth; student runs a day-night cycle and measures the two temperature curves diverging.

subtopics.title: Altitude
subtopics.idea: It gets colder as you go up, at a rate you can measure.
subtopics.design: Altitude transect: real lapse rate ~6.5 C/km; student measures temperature at stations up a mountain and derives the rate from their rows.

subtopics.title: Albedo
subtopics.idea: Bright surfaces reflect sunlight; dark ones absorb it.
subtopics.design: Albedo bench: real albedos (snow 0.8, forest 0.15, ocean 0.06); student measures absorbed power and the temperature reached for each surface.

subtopics.title: Day, night and the combined pattern
subtopics.idea: Heating and cooling combine over a day and a year to make the pattern we live in.
subtopics.design: Combined model: angle, albedo, thermal mass and day length together; student runs a full year at a chosen latitude and reads the seasonal curve out of it.

subtopics.title: Coastal versus inland temperature patterns
subtopics.idea: The coast stays mild while inland swings, because water moderates.
subtopics.design: California transect: coast, valley, desert with real thermal masses; student runs a summer day and measures the range at each site.

subtopics.title: The marine layer and coastal fog
subtopics.idea: Fog forms when moist ocean air is cooled below its dew point.
subtopics.design: Marine-layer bench: real upwelling sea-surface temperature and dew point; student watches fog form exactly when the air crosses its dew point, and burn off when it warms.

subtopics.title: The Sierra Nevada and rain shadow
subtopics.idea: Mountains wring rain out of air on the way up, leaving a dry shadow behind.
subtopics.design: Sierra transect: real orographic lifting and adiabatic cooling; student measures rainfall on the windward slope and the dryness beyond the crest.

subtopics.title: California's deserts
subtopics.idea: Deserts are dry because of where the air has been, not because they are hot.
subtopics.design: Desert bench: student traces the air's history over the mountains and measures its remaining moisture on arrival.

subtopics.title: The Pacific's moderating influence
subtopics.idea: The Pacific keeps California's coast within a narrow band all year.
subtopics.design: Ocean-influence bench: student toggles the ocean's thermal mass and measures how far the annual range widens without it.

subtopics.title: Putting California's weather together
subtopics.idea: California's weather is several effects stacked on one another.
subtopics.design: Combined state model: latitude, ocean, mountains and albedo all live; student explains a named city's climate by turning each effect off and measuring its contribution.

subtopics.title: Weather versus climate
subtopics.idea: Weather is what happens today; climate is the statistics of many years.
subtopics.design: Statistics bench: student samples a real daily series and computes 30-year means; watches a hot day fail to move the climate mean at all.

subtopics.title: Building climate from weather data
subtopics.idea: Climate is built by averaging weather over decades.
subtopics.design: Aggregation bench: student picks an averaging window and watches variance fall as 1/sqrt(n); finds where the record stops being noise.

subtopics.title: Reading climate graphs
subtopics.idea: A climate graph shows temperature and rainfall together, month by month.
subtopics.design: Climograph bench: student plots from real monthly rows and reads the wet and dry seasons off their own chart.

subtopics.title: Reading climate maps
subtopics.idea: A climate map turns many stations into one picture, and interpolation can mislead.
subtopics.design: Map bench: student sees the interpolated field and the actual station points, and measures where interpolation invents detail.

subtopics.title: Climate zones
subtopics.idea: Climate zones are defined by measured thresholds, not by looks.
subtopics.design: Koppen bench: student applies the real thresholds to their own data and classifies a site; a borderline site flips with a small change, which is the point.

subtopics.title: Convection cells from unequal heating
subtopics.idea: Unequal heating makes air rise in one place and sink in another.
subtopics.design: Convection-cell tank: real buoyancy from a heated equator and cooled pole; student measures the cell that forms and its speed.

subtopics.title: Circulation cells and prevailing winds
subtopics.idea: Rotation breaks one big cell into three, giving the belts of prevailing wind.
subtopics.design: Rotating-frame bench: student raises rotation from zero and watches one cell split into three, measuring the wind direction in each belt.

subtopics.title: An introductory Coriolis effect
subtopics.idea: On a spinning Earth, moving air and water curve.
subtopics.design: Coriolis bench: real deflection; student launches a parcel and measures the curvature against latitude, and finds it vanishes at the equator.

subtopics.title: Surface ocean currents
subtopics.idea: Surface currents are driven by wind and steered by rotation and coasts.
subtopics.design: Current bench: wind stress plus Coriolis plus basin geometry; student measures the gyre that emerges and its western intensification.

subtopics.title: Temperature, salinity and density in ocean water
subtopics.idea: Water's density depends on both temperature and salt, and that drives deep flow.
subtopics.design: Density bench: real equation of state; student sets temperature and salinity and measures density, then makes water sink by cooling or salting it.

subtopics.title: Heat redistribution: one combined model
subtopics.idea: Air and ocean together move heat from equator to poles.
subtopics.design: Combined transport model: student measures the heat carried by each and their total, and turns one off to see the pole-to-equator difference widen.

subtopics.title: Courtship behavior
subtopics.idea: Courtship behaviour improves the odds of successful mating.
subtopics.design: Behaviour bench: real signalling model with cost and detectability; student sets display intensity and measures mating success against predation risk.

subtopics.title: Nesting and parental care
subtopics.idea: Care after laying raises offspring survival at a cost to the parent.
subtopics.design: Care-tradeoff model: student allocates effort between clutch size and per-offspring care and measures surviving young — the optimum is found, not told.

subtopics.title: Flower structures and pollen
subtopics.idea: Flower parts are built for one job: getting pollen from one plant to another.
subtopics.design: Flower bench: student examines real structures and tests which pollinator each fits; mismatch measurably fails to transfer pollen.

subtopics.title: Pollination
subtopics.idea: Pollination is a transfer event with a measurable success rate.
subtopics.design: Pollination trial: real visitation and transfer probabilities; student changes pollinator abundance and measures seed set.

subtopics.title: Seeds and dispersal
subtopics.idea: Seeds travel by wind, water, or animals, and the method sets the distance.
subtopics.design: Dispersal bench: real terminal velocity for winged seeds, flotation, and gut passage; student measures the dispersal distance distribution for each method.

E4.title: Environmental and genetic factors in growth

subtopics.title: Environmental factors in growth
subtopics.idea: The same seed grows differently in different conditions.
subtopics.design: Growth chamber: real light, water and nutrient response curves; student grows identical genotypes in different conditions and measures the difference.

subtopics.title: Testing an environmental factor
subtopics.idea: To test one factor you must hold the others fixed.
subtopics.design: Four-chamber fair test on plants: the model genuinely confounds when two factors vary, and the confound is measured.

subtopics.title: Genetic differences and growth
subtopics.idea: Some differences are in the seed, not the setting.
subtopics.design: Genotype comparison: student grows different genotypes in identical conditions and measures the spread that remains.

subtopics.title: Comparing individuals across conditions
subtopics.idea: Comparing across conditions needs the same measurement every time.
subtopics.design: Protocol bench: student defines the measurement; inconsistent protocols produce measurably noisier comparisons.

subtopics.title: Separating genetic from environmental influence
subtopics.idea: Separating nature from nurture takes a design that varies each on purpose.
subtopics.design: Two-factor design: student runs genotype x environment and reads the separate contributions and the interaction from their own grid.

subtopics.title: Sexual reproduction
subtopics.idea: Sexual reproduction combines information from two parents.
subtopics.design: Gamete bench: real random assortment; student crosses parents and measures offspring variation across many trials.

subtopics.title: Why sexual offspring resemble but do not match parents
subtopics.idea: Offspring resemble both parents but match neither.
subtopics.design: Trait bench: student measures parent and offspring traits over many crosses and plots the distribution that results.

subtopics.title: Asexual reproduction
subtopics.idea: One parent can produce offspring alone.
subtopics.design: Asexual bench: budding, fragmentation, runners modelled with real rates; student measures population growth speed.

subtopics.title: Why asexual offspring are genetically identical
subtopics.idea: Asexual offspring carry identical information unless something mutates.
subtopics.design: Clone bench: student tracks a lineage and measures zero variation until a mutation event, whose rate is real.

subtopics.title: Comparing the two strategies
subtopics.idea: Each strategy wins in a different environment.
subtopics.design: Head-to-head: stable vs changing environment with a real pathogen; student runs both strategies and measures which population survives, and finds it flips with conditions.

subtopics.title: Genes as inherited information
subtopics.idea: Genes are instructions passed from parent to offspring.
subtopics.design: Information bench: student follows a gene through a cross and sees the trait it specifies appear in the offspring.

subtopics.title: Inheritance and variation among siblings
subtopics.idea: Siblings differ because each got a different combination.
subtopics.design: Sibling bench: student generates many siblings from the same parents and measures the spread of combinations.

subtopics.title: Why sexual reproduction produces variation
subtopics.idea: Variation comes from shuffling and recombining, not from blending.
subtopics.design: Shuffle bench: student watches independent assortment produce combinations, and sees a blending model fail to match the observed offspring.

subtopics.title: Why asexual reproduction preserves identical information
subtopics.idea: Copying without shuffling preserves the information exactly.
subtopics.design: Copy bench: student compares sexual and asexual lineages side by side and measures variation in each.

subtopics.title: Simple inheritance diagrams
subtopics.idea: A simple diagram can predict what offspring are possible.
subtopics.design: Diagram bench: student builds the cross diagram and predicts, then runs many offspring and checks their prediction against the counts.

subtopics.title: An introductory Punnett square
subtopics.idea: A Punnett square gives proportions you can test by counting.
subtopics.design: Punnett bench: student fills the square, predicts ratios, then runs 400 offspring and compares predicted to counted — sampling noise is real and visible.

subtopics.title: The components of the climate system
subtopics.idea: The climate system is atmosphere, ocean, ice, land and life, all coupled.
subtopics.design: Component bench: five coupled stocks; student disables one and measures how the others drift.

subtopics.title: Energy in and energy out
subtopics.idea: Earth's temperature settles where energy in equals energy out.
subtopics.design: Energy-balance model: real solar input, albedo and outgoing longwave; student changes one and watches the temperature find its new balance point.

subtopics.title: The natural greenhouse effect, descriptively
subtopics.idea: Greenhouse gases let sunlight in and slow heat leaving.
subtopics.design: Two-stream radiative model: student sets gas concentration and measures outgoing longwave at the top of the atmosphere and the surface temperature that results.

subtopics.title: A feedback, introduced conceptually
subtopics.idea: A feedback amplifies or damps whatever change starts it.
subtopics.design: Ice-albedo bench: real feedback loop; student nudges temperature and measures the amplification factor, then damps it and measures the difference.

subtopics.title: The climate system as interacting subsystems
subtopics.idea: The parts interact, so a push anywhere shows up everywhere.
subtopics.design: Coupled board: student pushes one component and traces the response through the real coupling arrows, measuring lag at each.

subtopics.title: Ice cores
subtopics.idea: Ice cores hold air from the past, so past CO2 can be measured, not guessed.
subtopics.design: Core bench: student drills, dates layers by counting, and measures CO2 from trapped bubbles against depth.

subtopics.title: Tree rings and coral bands
subtopics.idea: Rings and bands record yearly conditions in living things.
subtopics.design: Ring bench: student measures ring widths against a real growth-climate response and reconstructs past years.

subtopics.title: The instrumental record
subtopics.idea: Thermometer records show what has actually happened since they began.
subtopics.design: Record bench: student works with the real instrumental series, including station moves and gaps, and measures the trend with and without corrections.

subtopics.title: Sea level and sea ice
subtopics.idea: Warming shows up in sea level and shrinking ice.
subtopics.design: Sea-level bench: thermal expansion plus melt, both computed; student attributes the measured rise between the two causes.

subtopics.title: The Keeling curve
subtopics.idea: The Keeling curve rises every year and breathes every year.
subtopics.design: Keeling bench: student plots real monthly CO2 and separates the seasonal cycle (northern plant growth) from the trend, measuring both.

subtopics.title: Why independent evidence agreeing is the whole argument
subtopics.idea: Independent methods agreeing is what makes the conclusion strong.
subtopics.design: Convergence bench: student overlays independent proxies and measures their agreement; removing any one leaves the conclusion standing, which is the lesson.

F3.title: Causes: human activities and natural factors

subtopics.title: Greenhouse gases
subtopics.idea: Different gases trap heat with different strength and lifetime.
subtopics.design: Gas comparison: real radiative efficiency and lifetime; student compares equal masses of CO2, methane and N2O over 20 and 100 years and measures the effect.

subtopics.title: Fossil-fuel combustion and cement production
subtopics.idea: Burning fossil carbon moves carbon from rock to air.
subtopics.design: Combustion bench: real stoichiometry; student burns a measured mass of fuel and measures the CO2 produced and the carbon-reservoir shift.

subtopics.title: Agriculture and land use
subtopics.idea: Farming and land clearing move carbon too.
subtopics.design: Land-use bench: student converts forest to farmland and measures the carbon released from biomass and soil over decades.

subtopics.title: Natural factors
subtopics.idea: Volcanoes and solar changes act, but not on the scale or timing observed.
subtopics.design: Attribution bench: student adds real volcanic and solar forcing and measures how much of the observed trend they can and cannot explain.

subtopics.title: Comparing timescales
subtopics.idea: Natural changes take millennia; this one has taken a century.
subtopics.design: Timescale bench: student plots ice-age transitions and the modern record on the same axis and measures the rates.

subtopics.title: Correlation versus causation
subtopics.idea: Two things moving together does not mean one caused the other.
subtopics.design: Correlation bench: student is given real correlated pairs, some causal, some not, and must test with a mechanism and a controlled comparison.

subtopics.title: Reading a graph critically
subtopics.idea: How a graph is drawn changes what it seems to say.
subtopics.design: Graph-critique bench: same rows, different axes and baselines; student measures the apparent effect each version conveys against the true value.

subtopics.title: Applying this to climate data
subtopics.idea: Climate claims must be checked against the actual data.
subtopics.design: Claim-check bench: student tests specific claims against the real series and measures where each holds or fails.

subtopics.title: Evaluating a claim using multiple lines of evidence
subtopics.idea: A claim gets strong when several independent lines agree.
subtopics.design: Evidence bench: student assembles lines of evidence and the strength is computed from their independence and agreement.

subtopics.title: Spotting overstated and understated claims
subtopics.idea: Claims can overstate or understate; both are errors.
subtopics.design: Calibration bench: student compares a claim's stated magnitude against the measured one and scores the gap in both directions.

subtopics.title: Habitat change
subtopics.idea: When conditions shift, habitat moves, shrinks or disappears.
subtopics.design: Habitat bench: real climate envelope for a species; student warms the model and measures the area that remains suitable.

subtopics.title: Resource availability
subtopics.idea: Living things depend on resources that change with climate.
subtopics.design: Resource bench: student tracks water and food availability under a warming run and measures the population response.

subtopics.title: Plant growth and timing
subtopics.idea: Plants respond to timing cues, and warming shifts the timing.
subtopics.design: Phenology bench: real growing-degree-day model; student warms the climate and measures how many days earlier budburst arrives.

subtopics.title: Animal behavior and range shifts
subtopics.idea: Animals move, and their ranges shift with the conditions they need.
subtopics.design: Range bench: student runs a warming scenario and measures the range shift in km and where the species runs out of room.

subtopics.title: Existing adaptations and their limits
subtopics.idea: Adaptations have limits, and change can outrun them.
subtopics.design: Limits bench: student compares the rate of change to the species' real tolerance and adaptation rate and finds the point where it cannot keep up.

subtopics.title: Monitoring and indicators
subtopics.idea: You cannot manage what you do not measure.
subtopics.design: Monitoring bench: student places sensors and finds the sampling density where the signal becomes detectable above noise.

subtopics.title: Mitigation and adaptation
subtopics.idea: Mitigation reduces the cause; adaptation reduces the harm.
subtopics.design: Strategy bench: student allocates effort between the two and measures the outcome in emissions and in damage — both are computed.

subtopics.title: Defining the problem, criteria and constraints
subtopics.idea: A solvable problem has criteria and constraints stated as numbers.
subtopics.design: Problem-definition bench: student states targets and limits; the model refuses vague goals and scores only against numbers.

subtopics.title: Comparing and scoring alternatives
subtopics.idea: Alternatives are compared by scoring them against the same criteria.
subtopics.design: Scoring bench: student weighs alternatives against their own stated criteria; the ranking is computed from the weights they set.

subtopics.title: Technical claims versus value judgements
subtopics.idea: Data can tell you what will happen; it cannot tell you what matters most.
subtopics.design: Values bench: student separates the technical result (computed) from the value judgement (theirs), and the model refuses to make the second for them.

A.title: Atoms and the Structure of Matter

subtopics.title: Reviewing the particle model
subtopics.idea: Matter behaves as it does because it is made of particles in constant motion.
subtopics.design: Three-phase particle box driven by a real Lennard-Jones potential and Maxwell-Boltzmann speeds: student sets temperature and pressure and watches state emerge from the potential, never from a switch. Measures mean free path, density, diffusion coefficient. Fraud to avoid: sprites shuffled at a speed set by a slider.

subtopics.title: Why chemistry needs a sharper picture
subtopics.idea: The simple particle model cannot explain why substances react — you need what is inside the particle.
subtopics.design: Two-model bench: the same reaction run under a featureless-sphere model and an atom-with-structure model; the sphere model measurably fails to predict fixed mass ratios, and the student sees exactly which observation breaks it.

subtopics.title: Evidence that particles are real
subtopics.idea: Particles are real because their motion leaves measurable, quantitative traces.
subtopics.design: Brownian microscope with a real random walk: student measures mean-square displacement against time and particle radius, gets the linear MSD-vs-t law, and extracts Avogadro's number from Einstein's relation — a number, not a claim.

subtopics.title: Particles versus atoms
subtopics.idea: An atom is the smallest piece of an element; a particle in a gas may be a molecule of several atoms.
subtopics.design: Dissociation bench: student heats a diatomic gas past its bond energy and watches particle count double while mass stays fixed; measures both. This distinction is the whole subtopic.

subtopics.title: Scale of the atom
subtopics.idea: Atoms are about 0.1 nm across and the nucleus is 100000 times smaller still.
subtopics.design: True-scale zoom with a break glyph: student flies from a 1 mm grain to the nucleus with an honest metric ruler, and at the atom scale the nucleus is genuinely a dot 5 orders of magnitude down. Measures each step in metres.

subtopics.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
subtopics.idea: Three particles build every atom: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons outside.
subtopics.design: Assembly bench with real masses and charges: student adds each particle and watches mass (1.673e-27, 1.675e-27, 9.11e-31 kg) and net charge update; the electron's negligible mass share is measured, not asserted.

subtopics.title: Atomic number defines the element
subtopics.idea: Change the proton number and you have changed the element itself.
subtopics.design: Transmutation bench: student adds or removes protons and the element identity, chemical behaviour and spectral lines all change together; removing one from carbon genuinely produces boron chemistry in the reaction test.

subtopics.title: Mass number and isotopes
subtopics.idea: Isotopes share chemistry but differ in mass, and average atomic mass is a weighted average.
subtopics.design: Mass spectrometer: real magnetic deflection r = mv/qB separates isotopes onto a detector; student reads the peaks and abundances and computes the weighted average, matching the periodic table value they can look up.

subtopics.title: Building the model — early evidence
subtopics.idea: Rutherford's scattering forced the nucleus into existence: most alpha particles pass, a few bounce back.
subtopics.design: Gold-foil rig with real Rutherford cross-section (1/sin^4(theta/2)): student fires thousands of alphas and counts deflections by angle; the plum-pudding model, selectable, measurably cannot produce the large-angle events. Fraud: a scripted 'bounce'.

subtopics.title: Building the model — from shells to a cloud
subtopics.idea: Electrons occupy shells with definite energies, better described as clouds of probability.
subtopics.design: Spectral bench: student excites hydrogen and measures emission wavelengths, gets the Balmer series exactly, and derives the energy levels; then views the orbital as a probability cloud sampled from the real radial distribution.

subtopics.title: Why the model kept changing
subtopics.idea: Models change when new evidence arrives that the old model cannot explain.
subtopics.design: Model timeline as a testbed: student runs each historical model against each historical experiment and finds exactly which pairing fails. The verdict is computed from whether the model reproduces the data.

subtopics.title: Reading a cell of the periodic table
subtopics.idea: A periodic-table cell packs the element's identity, mass and structure into a few numbers.
subtopics.design: Cell reader: student picks any element and the cell's numbers drive a live atom build and a property lookup; changing the number in the cell changes the atom, proving what each figure means.

subtopics.title: Groups and periods
subtopics.idea: Elements in a group behave alike because their outer electron count is alike.
subtopics.design: Group bench: student reacts group 1 and group 17 elements with the same partner and measures reaction energy and product formula, finding the pattern follows the outer electrons — visible in the built atom.

subtopics.title: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
subtopics.idea: Metals conduct and bend, non-metals do not, and metalloids sit between.
subtopics.design: Property bench: student tests conductivity, malleability and lustre on real samples with real values (conductivity spanning 10^7 to 10^-15 S/m) and places each element on the measured boundary.

subtopics.title: Why the table is organized this way
subtopics.idea: The table is arranged so that repeating properties line up in columns.
subtopics.design: Sorting bench: student sorts 40 elements by mass and by measured property, and the periodic pattern emerges from their own ordering — Mendeleev's insight, rediscovered, including the gaps that predict unknown elements.

subtopics.title: Reactivity patterns across the table
subtopics.idea: Reactivity trends run down groups and across periods, and they follow structure.
subtopics.design: Reactivity bench: student runs the same reaction across a group and measures rate and energy released; the trend follows ionisation energy, which is shown from real data alongside.

subtopics.title: Element, compound and mixture
subtopics.idea: Elements have one kind of atom, compounds have atoms bonded in fixed ratios, mixtures have neither.
subtopics.design: Separation bench: student attempts physical separation (filtration, distillation, magnet) then chemical; mixtures yield to physical means, compounds do not. The classification is computed from what actually separated.

subtopics.title: Reading a chemical formula
subtopics.idea: A formula states exactly which atoms are present and how many.
subtopics.design: Formula reader: student types a formula and the molecule is built atom by atom, with a running mass; an impossible formula genuinely fails to assemble with a named reason.

subtopics.title: Subscripts versus coefficients
subtopics.idea: A subscript is inside the molecule; a coefficient counts whole molecules.
subtopics.design: Counting bench: student manipulates 2H2O versus H2O2 and the built structures differ completely; atom tallies and masses are computed from the actual assembled molecules.

subtopics.title: Counting atoms in a formula
subtopics.idea: You can count every atom in a formula, including inside brackets.
subtopics.design: Tally bench with real polyatomic formulas like Ca(NO3)2: student counts, then the model assembles and counts independently, and disagreement is shown atom by atom.

subtopics.title: Modeling a molecule from its formula
subtopics.idea: A formula is enough to build the molecule's real shape.
subtopics.design: VSEPR builder: student enters a formula and the geometry follows real electron-pair repulsion (bent water at 104.5 degrees, tetrahedral methane at 109.5); measures bond angles against reference values.

subtopics.title: Ball-and-stick models
subtopics.idea: A ball-and-stick model shows connectivity and angles clearly.
subtopics.design: Model bench: student builds with balls and sticks and measures bond angles and lengths against real values; the model's strength (geometry visible) and weakness (empty space exaggerated) are both measured.

subtopics.title: Space-filling models
subtopics.idea: A space-filling model shows the real size and packing of a molecule.
subtopics.design: Same molecule, van der Waals radii applied: student measures molecular volume and sees why the ball-and-stick view misleads about packing. Both models are shown from the same underlying coordinates.

subtopics.title: When there is no single molecule
subtopics.idea: Some substances are one endless lattice, with no molecule to point to.
subtopics.design: Lattice bench: student builds NaCl and diamond and discovers there is no repeating 'molecule' — only a unit cell and a ratio. Measures coordination number and density from the built lattice.

subtopics.title: Comparing molecular and lattice structures
subtopics.idea: Molecular substances melt easily; lattices do not, and structure explains why.
subtopics.design: Melting bench: student heats a molecular solid and an ionic lattice with real lattice and intermolecular energies, and measures the melting points that result (sugar ~186 C, salt 801 C) from the bonds being broken.

subtopics.title: Choosing the right model for the job
subtopics.idea: The right model is the one that answers your question, and every model hides something.
subtopics.design: Model-choice bench: student is asked four questions (shape, size, packing, reactivity) and must pick a model; the wrong choice measurably fails to answer, and the failure is shown.

B.title: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Matter

subtopics.title: Physical changes
subtopics.idea: In a physical change the substance is the same afterwards — only its form changed.
subtopics.design: Change bench: student melts, dissolves, crushes; the model tracks molecular identity throughout, and a reversal test recovers the original substance with mass and properties measured before and after.

subtopics.title: Chemical changes
subtopics.idea: In a chemical change atoms are rearranged into different substances.
subtopics.design: Reaction bench with real bond energies: student runs combustion and precipitation; bonds break and form, and the products' measured properties differ from the reactants'. Atom counts are conserved throughout, visibly.

subtopics.title: Cases that are easy to confuse
subtopics.idea: Some changes look chemical but are not — dissolving and melting fool people.
subtopics.design: Confusable cases: salt dissolving, wax melting, iron rusting, sugar caramelising, all measured with the same tests (recoverability, property change, energy). The classification is computed from the test results, never labelled.

subtopics.title: Properties before and after
subtopics.idea: Comparing properties before and after tells you whether a new substance exists.
subtopics.design: Property table bench: student measures density, melting point, conductivity, colour before and after and computes the verdict from their own table.

subtopics.title: Reversibility as a clue, not a rule
subtopics.idea: Easy reversal suggests a physical change, but some chemical changes reverse too.
subtopics.design: Reversibility bench: student attempts reversal on several changes, including a genuinely reversible reaction (hydrated copper sulfate); discovers the rule has exceptions, measured.

subtopics.title: Signs a reaction may have occurred
subtopics.idea: Gas, colour change, precipitate, temperature change and light hint at a reaction.
subtopics.design: Signs bench: five real reactions each showing different signs; student records which signs appear, and also meets a physical change that produces a sign (boiling makes bubbles) — the trap is the lesson.

subtopics.title: Analyzing property data before and after
subtopics.idea: Property data before and after is stronger evidence than appearance.
subtopics.design: Data bench: student collects the full property set for reactants and products and identifies which properties actually changed, computed from their rows.

subtopics.title: Identifying an unknown from a property table
subtopics.idea: An unknown can be identified by matching its measured properties to a reference table.
subtopics.design: Identification bench: student measures density, melting point, solubility and flame colour of an unknown and matches against a real reference; ambiguous matches require another measurement.

subtopics.title: Why appearance alone is not proof
subtopics.idea: Appearance can lie — dry ice smokes without reacting.
subtopics.design: Deception bench: several convincing-looking non-reactions; student must apply property tests to see through each. The model rewards measurement over looking.

subtopics.title: Naming a reaction from what goes in and comes out
subtopics.idea: A reaction is named by what goes in and comes out: synthesis, decomposition, combustion and the rest.
subtopics.design: Naming bench: student runs reactions and classifies from the actual reactant and product counts, computed from the balanced equation the model produced.

subtopics.title: Mass before and after, in a closed container
subtopics.idea: In a sealed container the mass never changes, however violent the reaction.
subtopics.design: Sealed-vessel balance: real reaction inside a closed flask on a balance reading to 0.001 g; student runs vigorous reactions and the mass is flat to the last decimal. Bit-for-bit conservation is enforced structurally.

subtopics.title: Mass before and after, in an open container
subtopics.idea: In an open container mass seems to change because gas left or joined.
subtopics.design: Open-vessel balance: same reactions uncapped; student measures the loss, captures the gas, weighs it and recovers the missing mass exactly.

subtopics.title: Atom-counting diagrams
subtopics.idea: Drawing the atoms before and after shows nothing is created or destroyed.
subtopics.design: Atom-counting bench: student builds the before and after molecules; the tally per element must match, and the model shows the mismatch when the student's equation is unbalanced.

subtopics.title: Why mass conservation follows from atom conservation
subtopics.idea: Mass is conserved because atoms are conserved — that is the whole reason.
subtopics.design: Linked bench: student changes the atom count directly and watches mass follow exactly; the two are the same fact viewed twice, and the model refuses to let them diverge.

subtopics.title: Applying conservation to an unfamiliar reaction
subtopics.idea: The rule holds for reactions you have never seen before.
subtopics.design: Unfamiliar-reaction bench: student is given a novel reaction and must predict the missing mass; the prediction is checked against the model's own conserved atoms.

subtopics.title: Energy added and particle motion, revisited
subtopics.idea: Adding energy makes particles move faster — until they start breaking free.
subtopics.design: Heating bench with the particle box: student adds measured joules and reads mean kinetic energy and temperature rising, then sees energy going into separation rather than speed at the transition.

subtopics.title: Forces between particles
subtopics.idea: Forces between particles decide whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature.
subtopics.design: Force bench: student sets intermolecular attraction strength and measures the melting and boiling points that result; real substances are provided as presets to compare.

subtopics.title: Reading a heating curve
subtopics.idea: A heating curve's plateaus are where energy goes into changing state, not raising temperature.
subtopics.design: Heating-curve bench: constant power heater, real specific and latent heats; student plots temperature vs energy added and measures both slopes and both plateau lengths, deriving latent heat from their own data.

subtopics.title: Why temperature plateaus during a state change
subtopics.idea: Temperature stalls during a state change because the energy is breaking bonds.
subtopics.design: Same bench with the energy ledger split live: student watches the joules routed to separation while kinetic energy holds constant, measured in real time.

subtopics.title: Predicting a heating curve for a new substance
subtopics.idea: If you know a substance's constants you can predict its curve before heating it.
subtopics.design: Prediction bench: student is given specific and latent heats for a new substance, predicts the curve, then runs it and measures the error in their prediction.

subtopics.title: Petroleum and plastics
subtopics.idea: Plastics are built from petroleum molecules rearranged into long chains.
subtopics.design: Polymer bench: student links monomers into chains and measures how chain length changes melting point and strength, with real values for polyethylene.

subtopics.title: Ores and alloys
subtopics.idea: An alloy is a mixture engineered to beat both its parents.
subtopics.design: Alloy bench: student mixes metals and measures hardness and melting point; real steel and bronze data show the alloy outperforming both pure metals, which is the surprise.

subtopics.title: Medicines and synthetic fibers
subtopics.idea: Synthetic molecules are designed for a job and tested against it.
subtopics.design: Design bench: student modifies a molecule's structure and measures the property it was designed for, seeing the structure-property link directly.

subtopics.title: Benefit and cost of a synthetic material
subtopics.idea: Every synthetic material buys a benefit at a measurable cost.
subtopics.design: Lifecycle bench: student weighs performance against energy, emissions and persistence with real numbers, and the trade-off is computed, never asserted.

subtopics.title: Comparing a natural and synthetic alternative
subtopics.idea: A fair comparison needs the same measurements on both alternatives.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: cotton vs polyester, or steel vs timber, measured on identical criteria the student sets; the winner changes with the criteria, which is the point.

subtopics.title: Criteria and constraints
subtopics.idea: A design problem is only real once its target is a number.
subtopics.design: Brief bench: student states the temperature change, time and cost limits; vague goals are refused by the model.

subtopics.title: Choosing a chemical process
subtopics.idea: Different chemical processes release or absorb different amounts of energy.
subtopics.design: Process bench: real enthalpies for several reactions (CaCl2 dissolution, ammonium nitrate, iron oxidation); student measures the temperature change each produces in a fixed mass of water.

subtopics.title: Collecting temperature data
subtopics.idea: The device's verdict is the temperature-time data it produces.
subtopics.design: Test rig: student runs their chosen process in their built device and records the real curve against their stated criterion.

subtopics.title: Modifying the design
subtopics.idea: Redesign means changing what the data showed was failing.
subtopics.design: Iteration bench: losses are itemised in watts (conduction, evaporation, mass of reagent); student changes the failing term and retests.

subtopics.title: Reporting the final design
subtopics.idea: A report states what was built, what was measured, and whether the target was met.
subtopics.design: Report bench: student assembles claim, their own recorded data and reasoning; the fit is computed from whether their data supports their claim.

subtopics.title: Naming the inputs
subtopics.idea: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide, water and light — nothing else.
subtopics.design: Input-starvation chamber: student removes CO2 (with soda lime), water, or light one at a time from a live leaf running a real light-response and Calvin-cycle model, and measures oxygen output collapsing for each. The input list is proved by subtraction, not stated.

subtopics.title: Naming the outputs
subtopics.idea: It puts out sugar and oxygen, and the oxygen can be caught and measured.
subtopics.design: Gas-capture rig: real O2 evolution from Elodea under water; student counts bubbles and measures volume against light intensity, and tests the gas with a glowing splint. Sugar is measured by iodine on the leaf.

subtopics.title: Where in the cell this happens
subtopics.idea: It happens in chloroplasts, which is why only green parts do it.
subtopics.design: Variegated-leaf experiment: student runs a real starch test on a leaf with green and white regions; only the chloroplast-bearing regions test positive, measured region by region.

subtopics.title: Photosynthesis as atoms rearranged
subtopics.idea: The atoms are not created — six CO2 and six H2O are rearranged into one sugar and six O2.
subtopics.design: Atom-tracking bench: student labels the carbon and oxygen atoms and follows them into products; the tally must balance, and the model shows exactly which oxygen atoms come from water (they do) versus CO2 (they don't) — the isotope result that settled it.

subtopics.title: Conditions that affect the rate
subtopics.idea: Rate rises with light and CO2 until something else becomes the limit.
subtopics.design: Limiting-factor bench: real light-response curve saturating near 400 umol/m2/s, plus CO2 and temperature; student raises one factor and measures the rate plateauing, then raises the true limiter and watches it climb again.

C2.title: Evidence for where a plant's mass comes from

subtopics.title: The intuitive but wrong answer
subtopics.idea: Most people think a plant's mass comes from soil — it is worth testing.
subtopics.design: Prediction bench: student commits to a source of plant mass before any data, and the commitment is recorded so the later evidence has something to overturn.

subtopics.title: Van Helmont's willow tree experiment
subtopics.idea: Van Helmont grew a tree for five years and the soil barely changed.
subtopics.design: Van Helmont rig on a real mass budget: student plants a 2.3 kg willow in 90.7 kg of soil, waters it for five simulated years, and weighs both; tree gains ~74 kg, soil loses ~57 g. The numbers are the historic ones, recomputed.

subtopics.title: What the soil-mass evidence actually shows
subtopics.idea: The soil evidence rules out soil — but it does not by itself name the source.
subtopics.design: Inference bench: student states what the mass data does and does not prove; the model accepts only conclusions the data supports, and rejects 'therefore water' as premature, which was Van Helmont's own error.

subtopics.title: Building the case for air and water
subtopics.idea: Air and water together account for the mass, and each can be tested.
subtopics.design: Isotope and gas bench: student runs labelled CO2 and labelled water and measures where each element ends up in the sugar and the oxygen; the carbon route is proved.

subtopics.title: Evaluating, not asserting, the conclusion
subtopics.idea: A conclusion is judged by the evidence behind it, not by how sensible it sounds.
subtopics.design: Evaluation bench: student scores several conclusions against the assembled evidence; the score is computed from evidential fit, and a true-but-unsupported claim scores badly.

subtopics.title: Naming the inputs
subtopics.idea: Respiration takes in sugar and oxygen.
subtopics.design: Respirometer: real O2 consumption by germinating seeds or yeast; student measures uptake against temperature and substrate, with a killed control that consumes nothing.

subtopics.title: Naming the outputs
subtopics.idea: It gives out carbon dioxide, water and usable energy.
subtopics.design: Output bench: student traps CO2 with limewater and measures the temperature rise in an insulated flask, quantifying energy released per gram of substrate against real values.

subtopics.title: Where in the cell this happens
subtopics.idea: It happens in mitochondria, in plant and animal cells alike.
subtopics.design: Cell-fraction bench: student separates organelles and measures which fraction consumes oxygen; only the mitochondrial fraction does, measured.

subtopics.title: Comparing photosynthesis and respiration side by side
subtopics.idea: Respiration is photosynthesis run backwards, in atoms and in energy.
subtopics.design: Side-by-side bench: both equations run live on the same atom pool; student sees inputs and outputs mirror exactly, and measures that energy is released in one and stored in the other.

subtopics.title: Respiration in plants and animals alike
subtopics.idea: Plants respire too — all the time, including in the dark.
subtopics.design: Day-night bench: student measures a plant's net gas exchange around the clock and finds respiration never stops; the compensation point is measured directly.

subtopics.title: Modeling a food molecule broken down
subtopics.idea: A food molecule is broken into smaller pieces, atom by atom.
subtopics.design: Molecule-breaking bench: student takes glucose apart step by step and the model tracks every atom; nothing may vanish.

subtopics.title: Modeling the atoms rearranged into products
subtopics.idea: Those atoms are reassembled into carbon dioxide and water.
subtopics.design: Reassembly bench: student builds the products from the freed atoms and finds the counts come out exactly right, with the balanced equation as the result of their own build.

subtopics.title: Energy released, not created
subtopics.idea: The energy was already in the bonds — respiration releases it, it does not make it.
subtopics.design: Bond-energy ledger: real bond enthalpies; student sums bonds broken and bonds formed and finds the difference equals the energy released, measured in kJ/mol.

subtopics.title: Comparing respiration to a familiar reaction
subtopics.idea: Respiration and burning are the same chemistry at different speeds.
subtopics.design: Two-rate bench: student burns glucose and respires glucose in the same model; identical products and energy, wildly different rates and control. Measures both.

subtopics.title: Applying the model to an unfamiliar food molecule
subtopics.idea: The same model works for fats and proteins, with different numbers.
subtopics.design: New-substrate bench: student applies the method to a fat and measures the higher energy per gram (~37 vs ~17 kJ/g), computed from its bonds.

subtopics.title: A carbon atom enters a plant
subtopics.idea: A carbon atom enters a plant as carbon dioxide and becomes sugar.
subtopics.design: Tagged-atom bench: student tags one carbon and follows it through the Calvin cycle into a real sugar molecule, timed.

subtopics.title: A carbon atom moves into an animal
subtopics.idea: Eating moves that carbon into an animal's own molecules.
subtopics.design: Feeding bench: student follows the tagged carbon through digestion into animal tissue, measuring how much is incorporated versus respired.

subtopics.title: A carbon atom returns to the air
subtopics.idea: Respiration and decay return it to the air.
subtopics.design: Return bench: student follows the tagged carbon out through breath or decomposition, and the loop closes measurably.

subtopics.title: Photosynthesis and respiration as linked opposite processes
subtopics.idea: The two processes are opposite halves of one cycle.
subtopics.design: Cycle bench: both processes on one carbon pool; student measures the flux each way and finds the balance point.

subtopics.title: Why plants run both processes
subtopics.idea: A plant must respire because photosynthesis only runs in light.
