subtopics.design: Necessity bench: student switches off plant respiration in the model and the plant dies overnight, measured — showing why it cannot rely on photosynthesis alone.

subtopics.title: Limiting resources
subtopics.idea: A population is capped by whatever resource runs out first.
subtopics.design: Limiting-resource bench: real logistic growth with several resources; student raises one and the population stalls until the true limiter is raised. Liebig's law emerges from measurement.

subtopics.title: Carrying capacity
subtopics.idea: Carrying capacity is the population a habitat can sustain indefinitely.
subtopics.design: Capacity bench: student runs a population past K and measures the overshoot, crash and recovery; K is computed from the resource supply, never typed in.

subtopics.title: Reading real population data
subtopics.idea: Real population data is noisy, and the pattern must be found in it.
subtopics.design: Real-data bench: student works with actual lynx-hare style series, smooths, and extracts period and amplitude from their own analysis.

subtopics.title: Predicting the response to scarcity
subtopics.idea: When a resource becomes scarce, the population responds with a lag.
subtopics.design: Scarcity bench: student cuts a resource and measures the delay before the population responds, and the overshoot that the delay causes.

subtopics.title: Competition for the same limiting resource
subtopics.idea: Two species needing the same limited resource cannot both win.
subtopics.design: Competition bench: real Lotka-Volterra competition; student sets overlap and measures exclusion or coexistence, finding the niche-difference threshold.

subtopics.title: Producers, consumers and decomposers
subtopics.idea: Producers make food, consumers take it, decomposers return it.
subtopics.design: Role bench: student assigns roles by measuring what each organism consumes and produces; removing decomposers genuinely locks nutrients up, measured.

subtopics.title: From food chain to food web
subtopics.idea: Real feeding relationships form a web, not a line.
subtopics.design: Web bench: student builds a web from feeding observations and then removes one species, measuring which others actually change — the web predicts, the chain does not.

subtopics.title: Trophic levels
subtopics.idea: Trophic level counts how many steps from the producer.
subtopics.design: Level bench: student assigns levels from the web they built and finds omnivores occupy fractional levels — computed from diet fractions.

subtopics.title: Why energy decreases at each level
subtopics.idea: Only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next level; the rest is respired or lost.
subtopics.design: Energy-transfer bench: student measures energy in and out at each level with real efficiencies (~10%) and finds where the rest went (respiration, waste, uneaten).

subtopics.title: Reading an energy pyramid
subtopics.idea: The pyramid's shape is a consequence of that loss.
subtopics.design: Pyramid bench: student builds the pyramid from their own measured transfers and discovers why long food chains are rare — the top level runs out of energy, computed.

subtopics.title: Matter cycling between organisms and the environment
subtopics.idea: Atoms cycle between living things and the environment endlessly.
subtopics.design: Cycling bench: student tags atoms and follows them out of and back into organisms; the atom count in the closed system never changes.

subtopics.title: Decomposers closing the loop
subtopics.idea: Without decomposers the loop breaks and nutrients lock up in dead matter.
subtopics.design: Decomposer bench: student removes decomposers and measures nutrients accumulating in litter while the living pool starves.

subtopics.title: The carbon cycle, introduced
subtopics.idea: Carbon moves through photosynthesis, respiration, decay and burial.
subtopics.design: Carbon-cycle bench: real reservoir sizes and fluxes; student perturbs one flux and measures where the carbon accumulates.

subtopics.title: The nitrogen cycle, introduced
subtopics.idea: Nitrogen must be fixed before life can use it, and returned as gas.
subtopics.design: Nitrogen bench: fixation, nitrification, uptake and denitrification as real rates; student removes fixers and measures the crash.

subtopics.title: Modeling matter and energy together
subtopics.idea: Matter cycles but energy flows one way — that asymmetry is the key idea.
subtopics.design: Combined bench: student tracks a matter tracer (which loops) and an energy tracer (which degrades and exits) in the same ecosystem, and the model structurally forbids energy from looping.

subtopics.title: Competition and predation
subtopics.idea: Competition and predation both limit populations, by different mechanisms.
subtopics.design: Interaction bench: real predator-prey and competition models side by side; student measures the different signatures each leaves in the population curves.

subtopics.title: Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism
subtopics.idea: Some relationships help one, both, or one at the other's cost.
subtopics.design: Symbiosis bench: student measures each partner's fitness with and without the other, and the relationship type is computed from the two signs, never labelled.

subtopics.title: The same pattern in very different ecosystems
subtopics.idea: The same interaction patterns appear in ecosystems that look nothing alike.
subtopics.design: Cross-ecosystem bench: coral reef, prairie and gut microbiome running the same interaction mathematics; student finds the shared pattern by measurement.

subtopics.title: Interactions that shift over time or condition
subtopics.idea: A relationship can change type when conditions change.
subtopics.design: Context bench: a mutualism that becomes parasitic under stress, driven by a real cost-benefit model; student finds the tipping condition.

subtopics.title: Interaction patterns and population change
subtopics.idea: Interaction strength shows up directly in how populations move.
subtopics.design: Coupling bench: student changes interaction strength and measures the resulting oscillation amplitude and period.

subtopics.title: Physical disruptions
subtopics.idea: Fire, flood and storm reset an ecosystem physically.
subtopics.design: Disruption bench: student applies a real disturbance of measured intensity and records which populations survive and how the structure changes.

subtopics.title: Biological disruptions
subtopics.idea: An invasive species or disease can disrupt as thoroughly as a storm.
subtopics.design: Invasion bench: student introduces a species with real competitive parameters and measures the native decline and any extinction.

subtopics.title: Constructing an argument from evidence
subtopics.idea: An argument from evidence names the claim, the data and the link.
subtopics.design: Argument bench: student builds a case for what caused an observed ecosystem change; the fit is computed from whether the cited data discriminates between causes.

subtopics.title: Succession after a disruption
subtopics.idea: After a disruption the community rebuilds in a predictable sequence.
subtopics.design: Succession bench: real succession model with facilitation; student runs decades and measures species turnover and the time to a mature community.

subtopics.title: Short-term versus long-term change
subtopics.idea: Some effects fade in a season; others last a century.
subtopics.design: Timescale bench: student measures recovery times for different variables (population, soil, canopy) and finds they differ by orders of magnitude.

subtopics.title: Naming ecosystem services
subtopics.idea: Ecosystems do measurable work for people: water, pollination, soil, carbon.
subtopics.design: Services bench: student switches off a service (pollinators, wetlands) and measures the cost in yield or flood volume, in real units.

subtopics.title: Threats to biodiversity
subtopics.idea: Habitat loss, overuse, pollution and invasives each reduce diversity.
subtopics.design: Threat bench: student applies each threat at measured intensity and records species lost, finding which threat this ecosystem is most sensitive to.

subtopics.title: Named solution categories
subtopics.idea: Protection, restoration, corridors and regulation are the standard tools.
subtopics.design: Solution bench: student deploys each with real cost and effect and measures outcomes.

subtopics.title: Evaluating competing solutions
subtopics.idea: Solutions are compared by scoring them on criteria you state first.
subtopics.design: Scoring bench: student sets criteria and weights, and the ranking is computed from their own weights applied to measured outcomes.

subtopics.title: A biodiversity solution for a real ecosystem
subtopics.idea: A real ecosystem needs a solution fitted to its specific threats.
subtopics.design: Case bench: a real ecosystem with its actual threat profile; student designs and tests a solution and measures diversity over decades.

subtopics.title: Igneous rock
subtopics.idea: Igneous rock forms when melt cools, and cooling rate sets the crystal size.
subtopics.design: Crystallisation bench: real nucleation-and-growth model; student sets cooling rate and measures the crystal size that results (fast quench = glass, slow plutonic = centimetre crystals), then identifies unknown samples by measuring their grains. Fraud: crystal size assigned by a label.

subtopics.title: Sedimentary rock
subtopics.idea: Sedimentary rock is built from pieces laid down in layers and cemented.
subtopics.design: Deposition tank: real settling by Stokes' law, so grain size sorts by current speed; student varies flow, watches beds form, then compacts and cements them and measures porosity lost.

subtopics.title: Metamorphic rock
subtopics.idea: Heat and pressure recrystallise rock without melting it.
subtopics.design: Metamorphism press: real pressure-temperature grid with mineral stability fields; student takes shale up the grid and measures the sequence slate-phyllite-schist-gneiss appearing at the right conditions, with foliation aligning perpendicular to stress.

subtopics.title: Identifying a sample from evidence
subtopics.idea: A rock's texture and minerals reveal how it formed.
subtopics.design: Identification bench: student measures grain size, sorting, layering, foliation and mineral content on unknown samples and the classification is computed from their measurements, never given.

subtopics.title: The energy that drives the cycle
subtopics.idea: The cycle runs on Earth's internal heat and the Sun's energy at the surface.
subtopics.design: Driver bench: student switches off internal heat (no melting, no uplift) or solar energy (no weathering, no transport) and measures which parts of the cycle stop.

subtopics.title: Physical weathering
subtopics.idea: Physical weathering breaks rock into pieces without changing its chemistry.
subtopics.design: Freeze-thaw rig: real 9% expansion of freezing water in a measured crack; student cycles temperature and measures crack growth and the number of cycles to failure, with rock strength as a real parameter.

subtopics.title: Chemical weathering
subtopics.idea: Chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves.
subtopics.design: Dissolution bench: real carbonic-acid attack on limestone with rate depending on pH, temperature and surface area; student measures mass loss over time and finds surface area dominates.

subtopics.title: Agents of erosion
subtopics.idea: Water, wind, ice and gravity all move sediment, each with its own signature.
subtopics.design: Agent bench: student measures the sorting, rounding and distance each agent produces, and identifies an unknown deposit from those measurements.

subtopics.title: Where sediment ends up
subtopics.idea: Sediment stops where the current can no longer carry it.
subtopics.design: Deposition bench: real competence-vs-velocity relation; student slows a current and measures which grain size drops out where, building a delta or alluvial fan from the physics.

subtopics.title: Soil formation
subtopics.idea: Soil is weathered rock plus organic matter, and it takes centuries.
subtopics.design: Soil bench: real weathering and organic accumulation rates; student runs centuries and measures horizon development, then measures how fast erosion can undo it.

E3.title: Geoscience processes across time and scale

subtopics.title: Fast processes
subtopics.idea: Some geological changes happen in seconds.
subtopics.design: Fast-process bench: earthquake slip, landslide, eruption at real rates; student measures displacement and duration.

subtopics.title: Slow processes
subtopics.idea: Others take millions of years, at millimetres per year.
subtopics.design: Slow-process bench: student measures uplift and plate motion at real rates (~5 cm/yr) and extrapolates to mountain building — the arithmetic is startling and student-computed.

subtopics.title: Constructing an explanation from rock layers
subtopics.idea: Rock layers record a sequence you can read.
subtopics.design: Strata bench: student applies superposition, cross-cutting and inclusions to a real section and derives the event order, checked against the model's own history.

subtopics.title: Combining fast and slow in one explanation
subtopics.idea: A real landscape is fast events written on slow ones.
subtopics.design: Combined bench: student runs slow uplift with occasional fast events and measures the resulting landscape, finding neither alone explains it.

subtopics.title: Spatial scale, from outcrop to continent
subtopics.idea: The same processes look different at outcrop and continent scale.
subtopics.design: Scale bench: student zooms from hand sample to continent with honest scale bars and measures how a feature's apparent shape changes with the scale of observation.

subtopics.title: Matching coastlines and rock types
subtopics.idea: Coastlines and rock belts match across oceans.
subtopics.design: Fit bench: student drags continents on a real spherical fit and measures the misfit in degrees at the continental shelf, discovering the shelf edge fits better than the coastline.

subtopics.title: Matching fossil distributions
subtopics.idea: The same fossils appear on now-separated continents.
subtopics.design: Fossil bench: real Mesosaurus, Glossopteris, Lystrosaurus distributions; student plots them and measures how the ranges close when continents are reassembled.

subtopics.title: Seafloor age and magnetic striping
subtopics.idea: The seafloor is youngest at the ridge and magnetically striped.
subtopics.design: Magnetic bench: real reversal timescale; student runs a magnetometer traverse and measures the symmetric stripes, then computes spreading rate from stripe width and reversal dates — a real velocity from their own data.

subtopics.title: Analyzing plate motion data
subtopics.idea: GPS and seafloor data give plate speeds you can calculate.
subtopics.design: Motion bench: student measures displacement over time from real station data and computes velocity vectors, then checks them against the ridge-derived rate.

subtopics.title: Reconstructing a simplified history
subtopics.idea: Running the motions backwards reconstructs the past.
subtopics.design: Reconstruction bench: student runs plate velocities backwards and measures how well continents reassemble at 200 Ma, with misfit computed.

E5.title: Plate boundaries and the landforms they build

subtopics.title: Divergent boundaries
subtopics.idea: Plates pulling apart make new crust and rift valleys.
subtopics.design: Divergent bench: real spreading with magma supply; student measures new crust created per year and watches a rift become an ocean.

subtopics.title: Convergent boundaries
subtopics.idea: Plates colliding build mountains or dive under, depending on density.
subtopics.design: Convergent bench: real density contrast decides subduction versus collision; student sets crust types and measures the mountain height or trench depth and the earthquake depth profile that results.

subtopics.title: Transform boundaries
subtopics.idea: Plates sliding past each other lock and then jump.
subtopics.design: Transform bench: real stick-slip with elastic strain accumulation; student watches strain build and release as earthquakes whose magnitude follows the accumulated slip deficit.

subtopics.title: Why hazards cluster at boundaries
subtopics.idea: Hazards cluster at boundaries because that is where the stress is released.
subtopics.design: Hazard-map bench: student plots their own modelled earthquakes and volcanoes and measures how tightly they follow the boundaries.

subtopics.title: Reading a plate-boundary map
subtopics.idea: A boundary map can be read to predict what a place will experience.
subtopics.design: Map bench: student reads a real plate map and predicts hazard type for named locations; the prediction is checked against the model's own physics.

E6.title: The uneven distribution of Earth's resources

subtopics.title: Mineral resources
subtopics.idea: Ore deposits form where specific processes concentrated a metal.
subtopics.design: Ore bench: real hydrothermal and magmatic concentration; student runs the process and measures the enrichment factor over crustal average.

subtopics.title: Energy resources
subtopics.idea: Fossil fuels need burial, heat and time in the right sequence.
subtopics.design: Fuel bench: real burial-history model; student varies burial depth and time and measures whether oil, gas or nothing forms — the oil window is discovered by measurement.

subtopics.title: Groundwater as a resource
subtopics.idea: Groundwater sits in pore space and moves slowly.
subtopics.design: Aquifer bench: real Darcy flow with measured porosity and permeability; student pumps and measures drawdown and recharge time.

subtopics.title: Renewable versus nonrenewable resources
subtopics.idea: Renewable means replaced on a human timescale — measured against use rate.
subtopics.design: Rate bench: student compares formation rate against extraction rate for each resource and the classification is computed from the ratio.

subtopics.title: Constructing an explanation for resource distribution
subtopics.idea: Resources are uneven because the processes that made them were uneven.
subtopics.design: Distribution bench: student runs the formation processes across a model continent and measures where deposits end up, explaining a real distribution map.

subtopics.title: Geologic hazards
subtopics.idea: Earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides come from Earth's internal energy.
subtopics.design: Geologic-hazard bench: real magnitude-frequency (Gutenberg-Richter) and energy release; student measures shaking intensity against distance and ground type.

subtopics.title: Weather-driven hazards
subtopics.idea: Storms, floods and droughts come from atmospheric energy.
subtopics.design: Weather-hazard bench: real storm energetics; student measures rainfall intensity, flood volume and the return period of each event.

subtopics.title: Tsunamis as a linked hazard
subtopics.idea: A tsunami is one hazard triggering another.
subtopics.design: Tsunami bench: real shallow-water wave speed sqrt(gh); student sets seafloor displacement and measures wave speed, arrival time and run-up height at a coast.

subtopics.title: California's own hazard profile
subtopics.idea: California's hazards follow directly from its geology and climate.
subtopics.design: State bench: real fault map, fire climate and coastal exposure; student measures the hazard profile at named locations from the underlying physics.

subtopics.title: A hazard's reach and duration
subtopics.idea: Hazards differ in how far they reach and how long they last.
subtopics.design: Reach bench: student measures footprint and duration for each hazard type and builds a comparison from their own runs.

subtopics.title: Frequency and location of past events
subtopics.idea: Past events show where and how often hazards strike.
subtopics.design: Catalogue bench: student works with a real event catalogue and computes frequency by location and magnitude.

subtopics.title: Probability, not certainty
subtopics.idea: Forecasts give probability, never certainty.
subtopics.design: Probability bench: student computes annual probability from recurrence and then runs many simulated decades, seeing the difference between a 2% annual chance and a guarantee.

subtopics.title: Reading a hazard map
subtopics.idea: A hazard map turns that probability into a picture you can act on.
subtopics.design: Map bench: student builds a hazard map from their computed probabilities and reads risk for specific sites.

subtopics.title: Early warning systems
subtopics.idea: Warning systems buy seconds or minutes by outrunning the hazard.
subtopics.design: Warning bench: real P-wave versus S-wave speeds; student measures the warning time available at each distance and finds the blind zone near the epicentre.

subtopics.title: Using data to forecast and inform mitigation
subtopics.idea: Forecasts are only useful if they change what people build and do.
subtopics.design: Application bench: student applies a forecast to a mitigation decision and measures the damage avoided.

subtopics.title: From vague want to measurable target
subtopics.idea: A vague want becomes a solvable problem when it gets a number.
subtopics.design: Target bench: student converts 'make it safer' into a measurable target; the model refuses to score anything vaguer.

subtopics.title: Criteria versus constraints
subtopics.idea: Criteria are what you want; constraints are what you cannot exceed.
subtopics.design: Definition bench: student separates the two for a real problem, and the model tests whether each entry is actually one or the other.

subtopics.title: Who the solution must protect
subtopics.idea: A solution must name who it protects — and who it does not.
subtopics.design: Coverage bench: student defines the protected population and measures who falls outside their solution's reach.

subtopics.title: Trade-offs already visible in the problem statement
subtopics.idea: Trade-offs are visible in the problem statement before any design exists.
subtopics.design: Trade-off bench: student states criteria and the model shows which pairs are in tension, computed from the physics.

subtopics.title: Defining a real mitigation problem
subtopics.idea: A well-defined problem makes the next steps obvious.
subtopics.design: Full-definition bench: student writes a complete problem statement for a real California hazard and it is scored for measurability and completeness.

subtopics.title: Generating more than one candidate
subtopics.idea: One idea is not a design process; you need alternatives to compare.
subtopics.design: Generation bench: student produces several genuinely different candidates and the model refuses to score a single one.

subtopics.title: A systematic scoring process
subtopics.idea: Scoring makes comparison honest by using the same criteria on every design.
subtopics.design: Matrix bench: student scores all candidates on their stated criteria and weights; the ranking is computed.

subtopics.title: Analyzing test data across designs
subtopics.idea: Test data decides, not preference.
subtopics.design: Test bench: each candidate is run through the same hazard model and measured; the data may contradict the student's favourite, which is the lesson.

subtopics.title: Combining the best characteristics of each
subtopics.idea: The best solution often combines the strengths of several.
subtopics.design: Hybrid bench: student combines features and measures whether the hybrid genuinely beats its parents — sometimes it does not.

subtopics.title: Presenting a recommendation with evidence
subtopics.idea: A recommendation states the choice, the evidence and the trade-off accepted.
subtopics.design: Recommendation bench: student presents with their own data; the fit is computed from whether the evidence supports the choice.

subtopics.title: Developing a model to generate data
subtopics.idea: A model lets you test a design before building it.
subtopics.design: Model bench: student builds a testable model of their mitigation and validates it against a known case before trusting it.

subtopics.title: A first round of testing
subtopics.idea: The first test tells you where the design fails.
subtopics.design: Round-one bench: student runs the hazard against their design and measures the failure mode and its threshold.

subtopics.title: Modifying and retesting
subtopics.idea: You modify the failing part and test again under the same conditions.
subtopics.design: Iteration bench: identical hazard conditions enforced so improvements are comparable; the model refuses to compare runs with different inputs.

subtopics.title: Naming the trade-off in each improvement
subtopics.idea: Every improvement costs something — usually money, mass or another risk.
subtopics.design: Trade bench: student measures the cost of each improvement in the stated currency and finds the knee of the curve.

subtopics.title: Converging on an optimized design
subtopics.idea: Optimisation ends when further change costs more than it gains.
subtopics.design: Convergence bench: student iterates until measured improvement per unit cost falls below their stated threshold, and the stopping point is computed.

subtopics.title: Distance vs displacement
subtopics.idea: Distance is the path walked; displacement is the straight line from start to finish.
subtopics.design: Walking track with a real path integrator: student walks a route and the model accumulates path length and the vector separately; a closed loop gives large distance and exactly zero displacement, measured. Fraud: two numbers that are not computed from the same trace.

subtopics.title: Speed vs velocity
subtopics.idea: Velocity carries a direction; speed does not, and the difference changes the answer.
subtopics.design: Same track, both quantities live: student walks out and back and finds average speed high while average velocity is zero. The two are computed from the identical trace.

subtopics.title: Reading a position-time graph
subtopics.idea: A position-time graph's slope IS the velocity.
subtopics.design: Graph bench with a real cart: student drives the cart and the graph draws from its measured position; then the student is given a graph and must reproduce the motion, scored on the trace they actually produce.

subtopics.title: Reference frames
subtopics.idea: Motion is only ever measured relative to a chosen frame.
subtopics.design: Two-frame bench: a walker on a moving train, measured from the platform and from the carriage; both traces are real and simultaneous, and the student reads two different, both-correct velocities.

subtopics.title: Calculating average speed
subtopics.idea: Average speed is total distance over total time, not the average of the speeds.
subtopics.design: Trip bench: student drives two legs at different speeds and computes average speed; the harmonic-mean trap is exposed by measurement (60 then 20 km/h gives 30, not 40).

subtopics.title: Acceleration as a rate of change
subtopics.idea: Acceleration is how fast the velocity changes, so it is a rate of a rate.
subtopics.design: Accelerometer cart: real a = dv/dt from the cart's own motion; student pushes and reads velocity and acceleration simultaneously, and finds acceleration can be zero while moving fast.

subtopics.title: Reading a velocity-time graph
subtopics.idea: On a velocity-time graph, slope is acceleration and area is distance.
subtopics.design: Velocity-graph bench: student drives, and the model integrates the area live to give distance, checked against the measured track position — the area rule proved by their own run.

subtopics.title: Constant vs changing acceleration
subtopics.idea: Constant acceleration gives a straight velocity line; changing acceleration bends it.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: constant thrust vs a real drag force; student runs both and measures the straight and curving velocity traces.

subtopics.title: Deceleration
subtopics.idea: Deceleration is acceleration pointing against the motion — same quantity, opposite sign.
subtopics.design: Braking bench: real friction; student brakes and measures negative acceleration, then reverses and finds the same sign convention holds.

subtopics.title: Connecting the two graph types
subtopics.idea: The two graph types describe one motion, and each is the other's slope or area.
subtopics.design: Dual-graph bench: student manipulates either graph and the other updates by real differentiation or integration; inconsistent pairs are impossible to create.

subtopics.title: Inertia
subtopics.idea: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless a force changes it.
subtopics.design: Frictionless bench: student sets friction to zero and launches; the object never stops, measured over minutes. Then friction is restored and the stopping distance is measured.

subtopics.title: Balanced vs unbalanced forces
subtopics.idea: Balanced forces leave motion unchanged; only unbalanced forces change it.
subtopics.design: Tug bench: real force summation; student adds forces and measures acceleration, finding zero net force gives constant velocity, not rest.

subtopics.title: Free-body diagrams
subtopics.idea: A free-body diagram shows every force on one object and nothing else.
subtopics.design: Diagram bench: student draws forces and the model runs their diagram; a wrong or missing force produces measurably wrong motion, which is the feedback.

subtopics.title: Friction as the reason intuition misleads
subtopics.idea: Things stop because of friction, not because stopping is natural.
subtopics.design: Friction bench: student varies surface and measures stopping distance against the real coefficient, extrapolating to zero friction and infinite distance.

subtopics.title: Applying the First Law to everyday scenarios
subtopics.idea: The First Law explains seatbelts, spilled coffee and everything that keeps going.
subtopics.design: Scenario bench: real cases run on the same physics; student predicts and then measures what the unrestrained object does.

A4.title: Forces, mass and change in motion

subtopics.title: Planning a fair test of force and motion
subtopics.idea: A fair test of force and motion holds mass fixed while force varies, or the reverse.
subtopics.design: Planning bench: the model genuinely confounds if both vary, and the confound is measured in the resulting data.

subtopics.title: The qualitative force-mass-acceleration relationship
subtopics.idea: More force gives more acceleration; more mass gives less.
subtopics.design: Relationship bench: student runs a series and plots a against F and against m, discovering the direct and inverse relations from their own points.

subtopics.title: Running the investigation
subtopics.idea: Running the investigation means repeating trials and recording honestly.
subtopics.design: Investigation bench: student runs replicates with real measurement scatter and computes means and spread.

subtopics.title: Comparing prediction to measured data
subtopics.idea: A prediction is tested by how close it lands to the measured value.
subtopics.design: Prediction bench: student predicts acceleration from F and m, then measures; the residual is computed and plotted.

subtopics.title: Communicating investigation results
subtopics.idea: Results are communicated as data, method and conclusion together.
subtopics.design: Report bench: student assembles their own rows into a report scored on whether the data supports the stated conclusion.

subtopics.title: Action-reaction pairs
subtopics.idea: Forces come in pairs that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
subtopics.design: Dual force-sensor bench: two carts collide and both sensors record simultaneously; the traces are mirror images at every instant, measured to the sample.

subtopics.title: Why the pair acts on different objects
subtopics.idea: The two forces of a pair act on different objects, which is why they never cancel.
subtopics.design: Pair bench: student assigns each force to its object and sees that summing forces on ONE object leaves a net force; assigning both to one object measurably breaks the motion.

subtopics.title: A common Third Law misconception
subtopics.idea: If the forces are equal, why does the small object fly off? Because equal force on smaller mass gives bigger acceleration.
subtopics.design: Truck-and-ball bench: identical force pair measured on both, then a = F/m computed for each; the wildly different accelerations from identical forces is the whole lesson.

subtopics.title: Applying the law to a collision-safety design
subtopics.idea: A safety design works by managing the force pair over time.
subtopics.design: Design bench: student adds crumple structure and measures peak force on the occupant, with the pair still exactly equal.

subtopics.title: Testing the design against criteria
subtopics.idea: A design is judged against the criteria that were stated first.
subtopics.design: Test bench: student's design is run against their stated peak-force limit and the verdict is computed.

subtopics.title: Defining criteria and constraints
subtopics.idea: Criteria and constraints turn a safety wish into a testable target.
subtopics.design: Brief bench: student sets a survivable peak deceleration (real human tolerance ~50 g brief) and mass and cost limits; vague briefs are refused.

subtopics.title: Crumple zones and impulse, conceptually
subtopics.idea: Impulse says a longer stop means a smaller force for the same change in momentum.
subtopics.design: Impulse bench: real F*t = m*dv; student lengthens the stopping time and measures peak force falling for the identical momentum change.

subtopics.title: Generating candidate solutions
subtopics.idea: Several different designs should be tried, not one.
subtopics.design: Generation bench: student builds crumple, airbag and restraint variants with real material properties.

subtopics.title: Systematic evaluation of designs
subtopics.idea: Designs are compared by running the same crash on each.
subtopics.design: Evaluation bench: identical impact conditions enforced; each design measured on peak force, intrusion and mass.

subtopics.title: Reporting the best solution and its trade-offs
subtopics.idea: Every safety gain costs mass, space or money — name it.
subtopics.design: Trade bench: student reports the winner with its measured cost, computed from their own runs.

subtopics.title: Kinetic energy and mass
subtopics.idea: Double the mass and you double the kinetic energy.
subtopics.design: Crush-block bench: student launches masses at a fixed speed and measures crush depth, finding the linear relation in their own points.

subtopics.title: Kinetic energy and speed
subtopics.idea: Double the speed and you quadruple the kinetic energy.
subtopics.design: Same bench at fixed mass, varying speed: the quadratic emerges from measured crush depths, never from a printed formula.

subtopics.title: Why speed has the larger effect
subtopics.idea: Speed matters more because it is squared.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student doubles mass then doubles speed and measures both outcomes side by side; the 2x versus 4x difference is measured.

subtopics.title: Interpreting the shape of the curve
subtopics.idea: The curve's steepening shape is the squared relationship made visible.
subtopics.design: Curve bench: student plots their own runs and reads the gradient at low and high speed, finding it grows.

subtopics.title: Applying kinetic energy to a collision scenario
subtopics.idea: Crash energy explains why speed limits matter more than they look.
subtopics.design: Scenario bench: student computes stopping energy at 30 and 60 km/h and measures the fourfold difference in crush and stopping distance.

subtopics.title: Gravitational potential energy
subtopics.idea: Lifting stores energy that height and mass decide.
subtopics.design: Lift bench: student lifts measured masses to measured heights, reads mgh, then drops and measures the speed at the bottom matching.

subtopics.title: Elastic potential energy
subtopics.idea: Stretching or compressing stores energy that the spring and the stretch decide.
subtopics.design: Spring bench: real Hooke's law and half-k-x-squared; student measures force vs extension, integrates the area, and checks it against the launch speed achieved.

subtopics.title: Potential energy as a property of a system
subtopics.idea: Potential energy belongs to the arrangement, not to the object alone.
subtopics.design: System bench: student tries to assign the energy to the ball alone and the model shows it takes Earth and ball together; removing either leaves nothing stored.

subtopics.title: Modeling potential energy as an arrangement changes
subtopics.idea: Change the arrangement and the stored energy changes with it.
subtopics.design: Arrangement bench: student moves objects and watches stored energy track the configuration, computed continuously.

subtopics.title: Potential and kinetic energy trading off
subtopics.idea: Kinetic and potential trade back and forth, and the sum stays put.
subtopics.design: Pendulum/ramp bench: both energies plotted live from state; the sum is flat to numerical precision until friction is enabled.

subtopics.title: Energy converted, not lost
subtopics.idea: In a crash the energy goes somewhere — deformation, sound and heat.
subtopics.design: Crash bench with a full energy ledger: student runs a collision and every joule is accounted into deformation, heat and sound, measured, summing exactly to the initial kinetic energy.

subtopics.title: Elastic vs inelastic collisions
subtopics.idea: Elastic collisions keep kinetic energy; inelastic ones convert it.
subtopics.design: Restitution bench: real coefficient of restitution; student sets it and measures the kinetic energy retained, from perfectly elastic to perfectly sticky.

subtopics.title: Tracing energy through a crash
subtopics.idea: You can follow the energy through a crash step by step.
subtopics.design: Trace bench: student steps through a collision millisecond by millisecond and watches the ledger shift between stores.

subtopics.title: Safety design and energy conversion
subtopics.idea: Safety features work by converting energy where it does no harm.
subtopics.design: Design bench: student routes energy into a crumple structure and measures the reduction in energy reaching the occupant.

subtopics.title: Comparing energy conversion across two collisions
subtopics.idea: Two crashes can be compared by their energy conversion.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student runs two collisions and compares the fraction converted in each, computed from their own ledgers.

subtopics.title: Energy is conserved
subtopics.idea: Energy is never created or destroyed, only moved and converted.
subtopics.design: Closed-system bench: student draws the boundary and the total is flat to the last joule; opening the boundary makes it appear to leak, and the leak is found.

subtopics.title: Tracking energy through a multi-step system
subtopics.idea: Through a multi-step system you can follow every joule.
subtopics.design: Chain bench: student tracks energy through four stages with real efficiencies and finds the total conserved at each step.

subtopics.title: Dissipation as spreading out, not disappearing
subtopics.idea: Dissipated energy is spread thin, not gone.
subtopics.design: Dissipation bench: student measures the temperature rise of the surroundings and finds the missing joules there, in real units.

subtopics.title: Applying conservation to a bouncing ball
subtopics.idea: A bouncing ball loses height because energy moved, not vanished.
subtopics.design: Bounce bench: real restitution; student measures each bounce height, computes the energy lost per bounce, and finds it as heat and sound in the ledger.

subtopics.title: Conservation as a check on a claim
subtopics.idea: If a claim breaks conservation, the claim is wrong.
subtopics.design: Claim bench: student tests claims (including a perpetual-motion design) against the ledger; the model shows exactly where the claim's energy would have to come from.

subtopics.title: Developing a model to generate data
subtopics.idea: A model generates data you can test a design against.
subtopics.design: Model bench: student builds a testable model and validates it against a known measured case before using it.

subtopics.title: Running a first round of testing
subtopics.idea: The first test finds the failure mode.
subtopics.design: Round-one bench: student runs and measures where and at what threshold the design fails.

subtopics.title: Modifying the model from test data
subtopics.idea: You change what failed, then test under identical conditions.
subtopics.design: Iteration bench: conditions locked so improvements are comparable; the model refuses to compare runs with different inputs.

subtopics.title: Naming the trade-off in each improvement
subtopics.idea: Each improvement trades something away.
subtopics.design: Trade bench: student measures the cost in mass, cost or another performance axis.

subtopics.title: A second round of modification
subtopics.idea: A second round shows whether the change actually helped.
subtopics.design: Round-two bench: student re-runs and the improvement is computed as a difference of measurements.

subtopics.title: Contact forces
subtopics.idea: Contact forces need touching: push, pull, friction, normal.
subtopics.design: Contact bench: student applies each and the model shows the contact point; separating the objects makes the force measurably vanish.

subtopics.title: Noncontact forces
subtopics.idea: Noncontact forces act across a gap: gravity, electric, magnetic.
subtopics.design: Gap bench: student separates the objects and the force persists, measured against distance.

subtopics.title: Sorting real scenarios
subtopics.idea: Real situations often mix both kinds.
subtopics.design: Sorting bench: student classifies real scenarios by testing whether the force survives separation — computed, not labelled.

subtopics.title: Attraction and repulsion
subtopics.idea: Some forces both attract and repel; gravity only attracts.
subtopics.design: Sign bench: student flips charges and poles and measures attraction and repulsion, then tries to make gravity repel and finds it cannot.

subtopics.title: Previewing the field idea
subtopics.idea: A field is how a force reaches across empty space.
subtopics.design: Preview bench: student maps the force at many points and the pattern that emerges IS the field, plotted from their own measurements.

subtopics.title: Electric charge
subtopics.idea: Like charges repel, unlike attract, and charge is conserved.
subtopics.design: Charging bench: real triboelectric transfer; student rubs materials, measures the charge on each, and finds the totals always sum to zero.

subtopics.title: Asking questions about electric-force data
subtopics.idea: Good questions about data ask what varies and what is held fixed.
subtopics.design: Question bench: student poses testable questions about the force data; the model runs only the well-formed ones.

subtopics.title: How distance affects the force
subtopics.idea: Electric force falls with the square of distance.
subtopics.design: Coulomb bench: real 1/r^2; student measures force at five distances and plots F against 1/r^2 to get a straight line — the law from their own points.

subtopics.title: How charge magnitude affects the force
subtopics.idea: Force is proportional to each charge.
subtopics.design: Charge bench: student doubles one charge and measures the doubling, then doubles both and measures the quadrupling.

subtopics.title: Static electricity and lightning
subtopics.idea: Lightning is charge separation released when the air finally breaks down.
subtopics.design: Storm bench: real charge separation and the ~3 MV/m breakdown field; student builds the field until the air breaks and measures where and when.

subtopics.title: Magnetic poles
subtopics.idea: Every magnet has two poles and they cannot be separated.
subtopics.design: Cutting bench: student cuts a magnet and measures that each piece still has both poles, however small.

subtopics.title: Magnetic materials
subtopics.idea: Only some materials are magnetic, and it depends on their structure.
subtopics.design: Material bench: student tests real materials and measures attraction; domain structure is shown for those that respond.

subtopics.title: Current produces a magnetic effect
subtopics.idea: A current makes a magnetic field around the wire.
subtopics.design: Oersted bench: real B = mu0*I/(2*pi*r); student varies current and distance and measures the compass deflection, deriving the relation.

subtopics.title: Building and varying a simple electromagnet
subtopics.idea: Turns, current and core all strengthen an electromagnet.
subtopics.design: Electromagnet bench: student varies each and measures lifting force, finding which factor gives the most gain per unit cost.

subtopics.title: Earth's magnetic field
subtopics.idea: Earth has a magnetic field, and a compass reads it.
subtopics.design: Earth-field bench: real dip and declination by latitude; student measures both and finds magnetic north differs from true north by a measured angle.

subtopics.title: Gravity is always attractive
subtopics.idea: Gravity only ever pulls.
subtopics.design: Attraction bench: student tries every configuration and measures that the force never reverses sign.

subtopics.title: Gravity depends on mass and distance
subtopics.idea: Gravity grows with mass and falls with the square of distance.
subtopics.design: Newton bench: real G*m1*m2/r^2; student varies each and measures, plotting to recover both relationships.

subtopics.title: Why everyday gravity goes unnoticed
subtopics.idea: Everyday objects do attract each other, just far too weakly to notice.
subtopics.design: Cavendish bench: student computes the attraction between two people (~1e-7 N) and then measures it with a real torsion balance that can just detect it.

subtopics.title: Mass vs weight
subtopics.idea: Mass is how much matter; weight is the force gravity exerts on it.
subtopics.design: Two-world bench: student takes the same object to Earth, Moon and Jupiter and measures mass unchanged while weight changes with real g values.

subtopics.title: Applying the gravity argument to new cases
subtopics.idea: The same gravity argument works for satellites, moons and falling apples.
subtopics.design: Application bench: student applies one equation to several cases and measures that it holds each time.

C5.title: Fields and action at a distance

subtopics.title: A field as something filling space
subtopics.idea: A field gives every point in space a value you could measure.
subtopics.design: Field bench: student places a test object anywhere and measures the force it would feel; the field is the map of those measurements.

subtopics.title: Mapping a field
subtopics.idea: Mapping a field means measuring it at many points.
subtopics.design: Mapping bench: student stamps measurements across a region and the field lines emerge from their own data, never pre-drawn.

subtopics.title: Investigating evidence of fields
subtopics.idea: Field lines are dense where the field is strong.
subtopics.design: Density bench: student measures field strength and line spacing and finds the inverse relation quantitatively.

subtopics.title: Energy transferred across empty space
subtopics.idea: Energy crosses empty space through fields.
subtopics.design: Transfer bench: student moves an object through a field and measures the work done with no contact anywhere.

subtopics.title: Fields as the unifying idea
subtopics.idea: Gravity, electricity and magnetism are all fields, which is why they share behaviour.
subtopics.design: Unification bench: student compares the three fields' maps and force laws side by side and finds the shared inverse-square structure, measured.

subtopics.title: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
subtopics.idea: Four numbers describe any wave, and period is just one over frequency.
subtopics.design: Wave tank with a real driven string: student sets frequency and amplitude and measures wavelength and period from the live trace with an on-screen ruler and stopwatch; f and T are checked against each other from their own measurements. Fraud: numbers printed rather than measured off the wave.

subtopics.title: Wave speed
subtopics.idea: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength, and the medium sets it.
subtopics.design: Speed bench: student changes frequency and watches wavelength change so that v stays fixed for a given medium, measured; changing tension changes v and both adjust.

subtopics.title: Amplitude and the energy a wave carries
subtopics.idea: Amplitude carries the energy, and energy goes as amplitude squared.
subtopics.design: Energy bench: student drives a wave into an absorber and measures energy delivered against amplitude, recovering the square law from their points.

subtopics.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
subtopics.idea: In transverse waves the medium moves across the travel direction; in longitudinal, along it.
subtopics.design: Dual-medium bench: real particle motion in both; student tracks a single tagged particle and measures its displacement direction relative to the wave's.

subtopics.title: Modeling wave behavior from data
subtopics.idea: A wave's behaviour can be predicted from measurements of it.
subtopics.design: Prediction bench: student measures a wave's properties, predicts its behaviour at a boundary, then tests.

subtopics.title: Three outcomes at a boundary
subtopics.idea: At a boundary a wave is reflected, absorbed, transmitted — usually all three.
subtopics.design: Boundary bench: real impedance mismatch; student sets the second medium and measures the three fractions, which always sum to one.

subtopics.title: Modeling absorption, reflection and transmission
subtopics.idea: The fractions depend on the two materials meeting.
subtopics.design: Material bench: student pairs media and measures the reflected fraction against the impedance ratio, deriving the relation.

subtopics.title: Why an object looks a particular color
subtopics.idea: An object's colour is the light it fails to absorb.
subtopics.design: Colour bench: real spectral absorption curves; student shines different spectra on the same object and measures the reflected spectrum, finding a red object under green light looks black.

subtopics.title: Refraction, introduced
subtopics.idea: A wave bends when its speed changes at a boundary.
subtopics.design: Refraction bench: real Snell's law; student varies the angle and index and measures the bend, plotting sin(i) against sin(r) for a straight line.

subtopics.title: Reading a wave-material interaction from evidence
subtopics.idea: You can identify a material from how it treats a wave.
subtopics.design: Identification bench: student measures reflection, absorption and refraction on an unknown and matches to a real reference table.

subtopics.title: Visible light as one narrow band
subtopics.idea: Visible light is a sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum.
subtopics.design: Spectrum bench with a true logarithmic axis: student zooms and measures that visible spans only 380-700 nm out of 20 orders of magnitude, with a break glyph making the compression honest.

subtopics.title: Ordering the spectrum by wavelength and frequency
subtopics.idea: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related across the whole spectrum.
subtopics.design: Ordering bench: student places bands by measured wavelength and frequency and finds the inverse ordering holds everywhere.

subtopics.title: A real use of each band
subtopics.idea: Each band is used for something that depends on its physics.
subtopics.design: Application bench: student matches band to use and tests it — microwaves heat water because of a real resonance, X-rays penetrate because of real attenuation coefficients.

subtopics.title: Why the whole spectrum travels at the same speed in a vacuum
subtopics.idea: All electromagnetic waves travel at c in a vacuum, whatever their energy.
subtopics.design: Race bench: student sends gamma and radio down the same vacuum path and measures identical arrival times, then adds a medium and measures dispersion appearing.

subtopics.title: Comparing energy across the spectrum
subtopics.idea: Photon energy rises with frequency, which is why some bands are dangerous.
subtopics.design: Energy bench: real E = hf; student computes photon energy across the spectrum and finds the ionisation threshold where damage begins.

subtopics.title: Sound as a longitudinal wave needing a medium
subtopics.idea: Sound is a pressure wave and it needs matter to travel through.
subtopics.design: Vacuum-jar bench: student pumps the jar down and measures the sound level falling to nothing as pressure drops, with the bell still visibly ringing.

subtopics.title: Pitch and loudness
subtopics.idea: Pitch is frequency; loudness is amplitude — they are independent.
subtopics.design: Tone bench: student varies each independently and measures the other unchanged, with a real spectrum display.

subtopics.title: Speed of sound across media
subtopics.idea: Sound travels faster in denser, stiffer media.
subtopics.design: Speed bench: real speeds (343 m/s air, 1480 water, 5100 steel); student times a pulse over a measured distance in each.

subtopics.title: The ear and the range of human hearing
subtopics.idea: Human hearing spans about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the ear converts pressure to signal.
subtopics.design: Hearing bench: student sweeps frequency and measures the audible band and the equal-loudness curve; the cochlea's real frequency mapping is shown.

subtopics.title: Echo and ultrasound
subtopics.idea: Echoes and ultrasound both measure distance by timing a reflection.
subtopics.design: Sonar bench: student times an echo and computes distance from the real speed of sound, then images a hidden object with a scanning pulse.

subtopics.title: How each signal encodes information
subtopics.idea: Analog varies continuously; digital encodes in discrete steps.
subtopics.design: Encoding bench: student sends the same signal both ways and measures the quantisation error introduced by digitising, against bit depth.

subtopics.title: Why digitized signals are more reliable
subtopics.idea: Digital survives noise because a step can be restored exactly.
subtopics.design: Noise bench: student adds real noise to both signals and measures the recovered fidelity; analog degrades continuously, digital is perfect until it cliffs.

subtopics.title: Noise and error correction, conceptually
subtopics.idea: Error correction adds redundancy so mistakes can be found and fixed.
subtopics.design: Correction bench: real parity or Hamming code; student corrupts bits and measures how many errors the code can detect and correct.

subtopics.title: Analyzing competing communication designs
subtopics.idea: Communication designs are compared on range, rate and reliability.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student runs designs through the same channel and measures all three.

subtopics.title: Integrating a wave-based communication device
subtopics.idea: A working device combines encoding, transmission and decoding.
subtopics.design: Integration bench: student builds an end-to-end link and measures the message that actually arrives.

subtopics.title: The lunar cycle
subtopics.idea: The Moon's phase is which part of its lit half we can see.
subtopics.design: Orbit bench: real geometry with the Sun fixed; student orbits the Moon and the phase is computed from the actual illumination angle seen from Earth. Fraud: a phase picture cycled by a timer.

subtopics.title: Modeling lunar phases
subtopics.idea: You can model the phases with a light, a ball and your own head.
subtopics.design: Physical-model bench: student positions the ball and measures the lit fraction from the Earth viewpoint, matching it to the real phase.

subtopics.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
subtopics.idea: An eclipse is one body's shadow falling on another.
subtopics.design: Shadow bench: real umbra and penumbra geometry; student aligns the three bodies and measures the shadow cone and where it lands.

subtopics.title: Why an eclipse does not happen every month
subtopics.idea: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees, so alignment is rare.
subtopics.design: Tilt bench: student sets the tilt to zero and gets an eclipse every month; restores 5.1 degrees and measures the eclipse frequency falling to the real rate.

subtopics.title: Tides
subtopics.idea: Tides come from the difference in the Moon's pull across Earth.
subtopics.design: Tidal bench: real differential gravity; student measures the pull on near and far sides and finds two bulges, then times high tides against the Moon's position.

subtopics.title: Axial tilt as the cause
subtopics.idea: Seasons come from the axis tilt, not from distance to the Sun.
subtopics.design: Tilt bench: student sets tilt to zero and measures seasons vanishing while the orbit stays elliptical; then varies distance alone and measures almost no effect. This kills the misconception by measurement.

subtopics.title: Angle of sunlight and day length
subtopics.idea: Tilt changes both the angle of sunlight and the length of the day.
subtopics.design: Angle bench: student measures solar altitude and day length at a chosen latitude through the year, and the energy per square metre that results.

subtopics.title: Why the hemispheres are opposite
subtopics.idea: When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the other tilts away.
subtopics.design: Two-hemisphere bench: student measures both simultaneously and finds them opposite at every date.

subtopics.title: Solstices and equinoxes
subtopics.idea: Solstices and equinoxes are the four positions where tilt aligns with the orbit.
subtopics.design: Marker bench: student finds the four dates by measuring day length and solar altitude, not by being told.

subtopics.title: Modeling the seasonal cycle
subtopics.idea: The whole cycle follows from tilt plus orbit.
subtopics.design: Full-cycle bench: student runs a year and reads the seasonal temperature curve out of the modelled insolation.

E3.title: Gravity in the solar system and galaxy

subtopics.title: Gravity holding orbits together
subtopics.idea: Gravity is what holds every orbit together.
subtopics.design: Orbit bench: real Newtonian gravity; student turns gravity off mid-orbit and the body flies off in a straight tangent, measured.

subtopics.title: Why an orbiting object neither falls in nor flies off
subtopics.idea: An orbit is falling forward fast enough to keep missing.
subtopics.design: Cannonball bench: Newton's own thought experiment made real; student raises launch speed and measures the trajectory going from falling to orbiting to escaping, finding both critical speeds.

subtopics.title: The Sun's dominant mass
subtopics.idea: The Sun holds 99.86 percent of the solar system's mass, which is why everything orbits it.
subtopics.design: Mass bench: student measures the mass budget and tests what happens when Jupiter's mass is raised until it competes.

subtopics.title: Moons, asteroids and comets
subtopics.idea: Moons, asteroids and comets all obey the same gravity.
subtopics.design: Small-body bench: student applies the same law to each and measures the orbits, including a comet's real eccentricity.

subtopics.title: The Milky Way, introduced
subtopics.idea: The Sun orbits the galaxy, which is held together by gravity too.
subtopics.design: Galaxy bench: student measures orbital speed against radius and finds the flat rotation curve that real galaxies show.

E4.title: The scale of the solar system

subtopics.title: The astronomical unit
subtopics.idea: An astronomical unit is Earth's distance from the Sun, and it makes the numbers manageable.
subtopics.design: Unit bench: student measures distances in km and AU and finds which is workable.

subtopics.title: Analyzing size and distance data
subtopics.idea: Size and distance data reveal how empty the solar system is.
subtopics.design: Data bench: student computes the ratio of body size to separation and finds it is thousands to one.

subtopics.title: Why a to-scale classroom model is nearly impossible
subtopics.idea: If Earth is a peppercorn, Neptune is a kilometre away.
subtopics.design: Scale bench: student picks a scale for the Sun and the model computes every distance and size honestly; the classroom is measurably too small, and the number needed is computed.

subtopics.title: Comparing planetary properties
subtopics.idea: Planets differ in size, mass, density and composition in patterned ways.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student measures and plots real planetary data and finds the rocky-versus-gas split emerging.

subtopics.title: Building a scale representation
subtopics.idea: A scale model must scale sizes and distances by the same factor.
subtopics.design: Model bench: student builds a scale model and the model catches any inconsistent scaling by measurement.

E5.title: Rock strata and the geologic time scale

subtopics.title: Superposition
subtopics.idea: Lower layers are older, unless something disturbed them.
subtopics.design: Superposition bench: student reads a section and orders events, then meets an overturned sequence where the rule alone fails.

subtopics.title: Index fossils and unconformities
subtopics.idea: Index fossils date a layer; unconformities mark missing time.
subtopics.design: Correlation bench: student correlates sections using real index fossils and measures the time missing at each unconformity.

subtopics.title: Reading strata as a record
subtopics.idea: Strata are a record you can read in order.
subtopics.design: Reading bench: student derives a full event history from a real section, checked against the model's own generated history.

subtopics.title: Eons, eras and periods
subtopics.idea: The time scale divides Earth's history by what the rocks record.
subtopics.design: Time-scale bench: student places their measured events on the real scale and sees the proportions of Earth's history each division occupies.

subtopics.title: Constructing an explanation from strata evidence
subtopics.idea: An explanation from strata cites the specific layers it rests on.
subtopics.design: Explanation bench: student builds an account and the fit is computed from whether the cited layers actually support it.

subtopics.title: Relative vs absolute dating
subtopics.idea: Relative dating gives order; absolute dating gives years.
subtopics.design: Two-method bench: student applies both to the same section and measures what each can and cannot tell them.

subtopics.title: Radiometric dating, conceptually
subtopics.idea: Radioactive decay is a clock because half-life is constant.
subtopics.design: Decay bench: real exponential decay with genuine statistical randomness per atom; student measures the half-life from their own counts and finds it constant regardless of starting amount or temperature.

subtopics.title: Combining relative and absolute evidence
subtopics.idea: The strongest dating combines order from layers with years from isotopes.
subtopics.design: Combined bench: student dates a section using both and measures how the combination narrows the uncertainty.

subtopics.title: The 4.6-billion-year figure
subtopics.idea: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, from meteorite and rock dating.
subtopics.design: Age bench: student dates the oldest samples and measures the convergence of independent methods on 4.54 Ga.

subtopics.title: Evaluating a dating claim
subtopics.idea: A dating claim is checked against method, assumptions and uncertainty.
subtopics.design: Evaluation bench: student tests claims against whether the method suits the age range and whether the sample was closed.

subtopics.title: A mutation as a change to genetic information
subtopics.idea: A mutation is a change in the genetic information.
subtopics.design: Sequence bench: student mutates a real sequence and the model shows the resulting protein change, computed from the actual codon table.

subtopics.title: Beneficial, harmful and neutral outcomes
subtopics.idea: A mutation can help, harm, or do nothing, depending on context.
subtopics.design: Outcome bench: student mutates and measures fitness in a specified environment; the same mutation can flip sign when the environment changes.

subtopics.title: Why most mutations are neutral
subtopics.idea: Most mutations are neutral because most of the genome tolerates change.
subtopics.design: Distribution bench: student runs many random mutations and measures the distribution of effects, finding the neutral majority.

subtopics.title: Mutation as the ultimate source of variation
subtopics.idea: Without mutation there is no new variation for selection to act on.
subtopics.design: Source bench: student switches mutation off and measures variation draining away over generations until adaptation stops.

subtopics.title: Tracing a trait to a mutation
subtopics.idea: A trait can be traced back to the specific change that produced it.
subtopics.design: Tracing bench: student follows a trait to its causal mutation through the model's own lineage records.

F2.title: Fossil evidence of change over time

subtopics.title: How a fossil forms
subtopics.idea: Fossilisation needs quick burial and the right conditions, so it is rare.
subtopics.design: Taphonomy bench: real preservation probabilities by environment; student measures what fraction of organisms fossilise and which body parts survive.

subtopics.title: Order of appearance and extinction
subtopics.idea: The fossil record shows groups appearing and disappearing in order.
subtopics.design: Record bench: student measures first and last appearances across layers and builds the range chart from their own data.

subtopics.title: Transitional forms
subtopics.idea: Transitional forms show intermediate features in the right layers.
subtopics.design: Transitional bench: student measures features across a real sequence and finds the intermediate states in the intermediate layers.

subtopics.title: Placing fossils on the time scale
subtopics.idea: Fossils are placed by the age of the rock that holds them.
subtopics.design: Placement bench: student dates the rock and places the fossil, and the resulting order is computed.

subtopics.title: Analyzing fossil-record data
subtopics.idea: Patterns of change over time come out of the data, not out of belief.
subtopics.design: Analysis bench: student measures trends in real fossil data and computes the rate of change.

subtopics.title: Homologous structures
subtopics.idea: Homologous structures share a plan because they share an ancestor.
subtopics.design: Homology bench: student aligns limb bones across species and measures the correspondence, bone by bone.

subtopics.title: Analogous and vestigial structures
subtopics.idea: Analogous structures share a job, not an ancestor; vestigial ones have lost their job.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student measures structural correspondence and finds analogous structures differ underneath despite similar function.

subtopics.title: Shared ancestry vs convergence
subtopics.idea: Shared plan means ancestry; shared function alone does not.
subtopics.design: Discrimination bench: student is given pairs and must decide using structural evidence; the verdict is computed from the measured correspondence.

subtopics.title: Comparing early development across species
subtopics.idea: Embryos of related species resemble each other more than the adults do.
subtopics.design: Development bench: student compares developmental stages and measures where the divergence happens.

subtopics.title: Inferring evolutionary relationships
subtopics.idea: Relationships are inferred by counting shared derived features.
subtopics.design: Tree bench: student builds a tree from their own measured character matrix; the tree is computed, not drawn for them.

subtopics.title: Variation, survival and heritability
subtopics.idea: Selection needs variation, that variation must affect survival, and it must be heritable.
subtopics.design: Three-condition bench: student switches each condition off and measures adaptation failing in each case — all three are necessary, proved by removal.

subtopics.title: A fully worked real case
subtopics.idea: A real case shows the whole mechanism working.
subtopics.design: Peppered-moth bench with real predation data: student sets soot level and measures allele frequency shifting over generations, matching the historical record.

subtopics.title: Differential survival and reproduction
subtopics.idea: Some individuals leave more offspring, and that is what changes the population.
subtopics.design: Reproduction bench: student measures differential reproduction directly and watches the trait frequency follow it.

subtopics.title: Selection acts on populations, never on an individual's lifetime
subtopics.idea: An individual does not evolve; the population's proportions shift.
subtopics.design: Individual-vs-population bench: student tracks one organism (which never changes) and the population (which does), simultaneously — the misconception dies by measurement.

subtopics.title: Constructing an evidence-based explanation
subtopics.idea: An evolutionary explanation cites variation, selection pressure and heritability.
subtopics.design: Explanation bench: student builds the account and it is scored on whether their own run's data supports each part.

F5.title: Artificial selection and adaptation over time

subtopics.title: Selective breeding
subtopics.idea: Breeders choose the parents, and the population follows.
subtopics.design: Breeding bench: student selects parents by trait and measures the shift over generations, with real heritability.

subtopics.title: The same mechanism, a human selector
subtopics.idea: Artificial and natural selection are the same mechanism with a different selector.
subtopics.design: Comparison bench: student runs both on the same population and measures identical mathematics with a different selection criterion.

subtopics.title: Technologies influencing inheritance
subtopics.idea: Modern technologies change inheritance more directly.
subtopics.design: Technology bench: student compares breeding, hybridisation and direct editing and measures the generations each needs to reach a target.

subtopics.title: Tracking a trait's proportion across generations
subtopics.idea: A trait's proportion can be counted generation by generation.
subtopics.design: Frequency bench: student counts and plots allele frequency across generations from their own runs.

subtopics.title: Predicting a population's future trait proportions
subtopics.idea: If you know the selection pressure you can predict the trend.
subtopics.design: Prediction bench: student predicts future proportions from measured selection strength, then runs and measures the error.

subtopics.title: Population growth as one multiplier
subtopics.idea: More people means more impact, all else equal.
subtopics.design: Population bench: real growth model; student varies population and measures resource use and emissions.

subtopics.title: Per-capita consumption as the other multiplier
subtopics.idea: How much each person uses matters as much as how many people there are.
subtopics.design: Consumption bench: student varies per-capita use and finds it can outweigh population change, measured on the same impact axis.

subtopics.title: Constructing an argument from real data
subtopics.idea: An argument about impact must rest on the actual data.
subtopics.design: Argument bench: student builds a case from real population and consumption data; the fit is computed.

subtopics.title: Impact on biodiversity specifically
subtopics.idea: Human activity reduces biodiversity through specific, measurable mechanisms.
subtopics.design: Impact bench: student applies habitat loss, harvest and pollution at measured intensities and records species lost.

subtopics.title: Presenting management options with trade-offs
subtopics.idea: Every management option protects something and costs something.
subtopics.design: Options bench: student compares options on their own stated criteria and reports the trade-off measured, not asserted.
